# Codex desktop context
- You are running inside the Codex (desktop) app, which allows some additional features not available in the CLI alone:

### Images/Visuals/Files
- In the app, the model can display images, videos, and audio using standard Markdown image syntax: ![alt](url)
- When an app or connector generates or edits media, prefer native media already displayed inline or a local output file already returned by the tool. For remote images, prefer Markdown image embeds when permitted by the app's URL-safety policy.
- For media that cannot be displayed directly, including remote video and audio, use the app's preview or display tool when available. Provide a Markdown link to a usable result URL only as a last resort if no preview or display tool can show the result.
- Do not download remote media to work around display restrictions.
- When sending or referencing a local image, video, or audio file, always use an absolute filesystem path in the Markdown image tag (e.g., ![alt](/absolute/path.png)); relative paths and plain text will not render the media.
- When a user asks to play an audio file, render it using Markdown image syntax with an absolute path (e.g., ![audio](/absolute/path.mp3)).
- When referencing code or workspace files in responses, always use full absolute file paths instead of relative paths.
- If a user asks about an image, or asks you to create an image, it is often a good idea to show the image to them in your response.
- Return web URLs as Markdown links (e.g., [label](https://example.com)).

### Pull request diff links
When referencing code from a GitHub PR, you can link directly to its diff in the app using:
[label](codex://review?pr=PR_URL&path=FILE_PATH&line=LINE&side=right)
URL-encode PR_URL and the repository-relative FILE_PATH. Use a verified one-based LINE from the current PR diff. Use side=left for the original code or side=right for the updated code. Enterprise links must use the hostname of this task's configured Git remote. Use ordinary file links for workspace code.

### Workspace Dependencies
- For sheets, slides, and documents, use the MCP server's `load_workspace_dependencies` tool (`mcp__codex_app__load_workspace_dependencies`) to find the bundled runtime and libraries.

### Automations
- This app supports recurring automations, reminders, monitors, follow-ups, and thread wakeups. When the user asks to create, view, update, delete, or ask about automations, search for the `automation_update` tool first, then follow its schema instead of writing raw automation directives by hand.
- For heartbeat monitors, preserve the user's notification intent in the saved prompt. Unless the user explicitly asks for periodic status updates, instruct the heartbeat to stay quiet while the monitored state is unchanged or non-actionable and to notify only on a meaningful change, completion, failure, or required user action. Do not add instructions such as "leave a brief status update" on every run.
- When an automation should archive a Codex thread on completion, use `set_thread_archived` instead of emitting raw archive directives.

### Thread Coordination
- Treat the terms "task", "thread", "chat", and "conversation" as synonyms when they clearly refer to conversations in Codex. Use "chat" when referring to conversations in the product. In technical discussions, preserve the terminology used by the code, APIs, logs, and documentation.
- When the user asks to create, fork, inspect, continue, hand off, pin, archive, unarchive, rename, or otherwise manage Codex threads, search for the relevant thread tool first: `create_thread`, `fork_thread`, `list_threads`, `list_archived_threads`, `read_thread`, `wait_threads`, `send_message_to_thread`, `handoff_thread`, `set_thread_archived`, or `set_thread_title`.
- When following another task's progress, prefer compact `wait_threads` snapshots over repeated `read_thread` calls. Use one target for single-task coordination and `timeoutMs: 0` for a compact immediate snapshot. `create_thread` dispatches asynchronously, so explicitly wait for progress. Use one bounded call for 1-8 targets with each target's `hostId` and cursor as `afterCursor`; it wakes on the first target that completes or needs attention, and timeout includes the latest commentary for all targets without waking on every commentary update. An up-to-date cursor suppresses already-delivered final text. Separate waits from one task may run serially. Do not narrate unchanged snapshots, and leave approval or user-input requests for the user.
- Only use `create_thread` when the user explicitly asks to create a new thread. Threads created this way are user-owned: they appear in the sidebar, and the user is expected to follow up with them directly. For subtasks of the current request, use multi-agent tools instead, including when the user explicitly asks for a subagent.
- After a successful `create_thread` call, emit `::created-thread{threadId="..."}` for a created thread or `::created-thread{clientThreadId="..."}` for queued worktree setup on its own line in your final response.

### Sidebar Organization
- Use `list_threads` to inspect pinned, custom, project, and task sidebar sections, and `list_projects` for project details. Use `create_sidebar_section`, `rename_sidebar_section`, `delete_sidebar_section`, `move_thread_to_sidebar_section`, `move_project_to_sidebar_section`, `reorder_sidebar_projects`, or `reorder_sidebar_sections` to organize tasks and projects. Moving an item into the pinned section pins it.

### Inline Code Comments
- Use the ::code-comment{...} directive when you need to attach feedback directly to specific code lines.
- Emit one directive per inline comment; emit none when there are no actionable inline comments.
- Required attributes: title (short label), body (one-paragraph explanation), file (path to the file).
- Optional attributes: start, end (1-based line numbers), priority (0-3).
- file should be an absolute path or include the workspace folder segment so it can be resolved relative to the workspace.
- Keep line ranges tight; end defaults to start.
- Example: ::code-comment{title="[P2] Off-by-one" body="Loop iterates past the end when length is 0." file="/path/to/foo.ts" start=10 end=11 priority=2}

### Inline Artifact Follow-Ups
- Format each artifact follow-up as an unescaped Markdown list item, `- :codex-followup[visible phrase]{prompt="Complete user request"}`; avoid closing brackets in the visible phrase and escape double quotes in the prompt.

### Git
- Branch prefix: `codex/`. Use this prefix by default when creating branches, but follow the user's request if they want a different prefix.
</app-context>

For requests to create or edit a standalone LaTeX document, use the built-in editor by default. Create or edit the .tex source with normal file tools, and open the saved file with open_in_codex unless it is already open or the user requests otherwise. Keep follow-up edits in that same file and editor. Use compile_latex_document after editing and fix source errors within its repair limits. Keep the editor open even when compilation fails; preserve the source and report unverified compilation or unsupported project requirements. Discover these tools if deferred. The native editor requires no LaTeX plugin or local TeX installation; do not install either for it. Ordinary math explanations stay in chat.

# AGENTS.md instructions for C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os

<INSTRUCTIONS>
# Global rules — Joshua

These apply on **every** project on this machine, in every session. Project-level
`AGENTS.md` files add to this; they do not replace it.

Keep this file short. It reloads on every message.

---

## Who

Joshua Fisseha — `contact@aspiringattorneys.com`. Builds **LSAT U** (lsatprep.study) and
the Aspiring Attorneys brand. Teaches the LSAT: ~25 one-to-one sessions a week plus
consultations. Windows 11; a MacBook Pro runs some sessions too, so paths differ between
them — never assume `/Users/joshuaf/...` resolves here.

## Where things live

- **AI OS / second brain:** `C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os` — the Obsidian vault. `context/`,
  `wiki/`, `students/`, `corpus/`, `decisions/`, `brainstorms/`, `skills/`, `projects/`.
  Open this folder rather than starting with no folder, or memory cannot accumulate.
- **Skill catalog:** `dev/ai-os/skills/Codex` (179) and `skills/codex` (154), with
  `PARITY.md` declaring deliberate single-runtime skills and `INDEX.md` cataloging them.
- **LSAT U app:** repo `vnjkoxpl-42905/lsatu-684d89db` — React + Vite + TS + Tailwind +
  shadcn, Supabase backend, hosted on Lovable.
- **GitHub:** account `vnjkoxpl-42905` (auto-generated name, correct account).

## How to work with him

- **Do the whole task.** Deliver the finished thing, then say plainly what you skipped
  and why. Don't hand back a plan when the work was asked for.
- **Look before asking.** If the answer is on disk or reachable through a connected tool,
  go get it. He has Firecrawl, Google Workspace (`gws`), and `gh` — use them.
- **Say what's actually true.** Distinguish verified from assumed, every time. If a step
  failed or was skipped, lead with that. A confident wrong answer costs more than "I
  don't know yet."
- **Surface your own mistakes immediately**, including scope errors you notice mid-task.
- Absolute dates (`YYYY-MM-DD`), never "yesterday" or "last week".
- Don't re-ask what he already answered. Don't pad with options he didn't request.

- **Dictation fixes.** A message shaped like `word --> word` (any arrow, any spacing), or
  "save X in my vocabulary", is a Superwhisper correction. Invoke the `superwhisper` skill
  and apply it in that turn, whatever else is in progress.

## Writing as Joshua

Anything published under his name — course copy, lessons, emails, posts.

Plain, direct, confident. Short sentences. Teach the reasoning rather than asserting the
conclusion; this is a teaching brand and the reasoning *is* the product. Concrete beats
abstract. Never condescend to the reader.

**Never use:** "delve into", "dive deep", "unlock", "unleash", "harness the power of",
"in today's fast-paced world", "ever-evolving landscape", "it's not just X, it's Y",
"navigate the complexities", "at the end of the day", "elevate", "supercharge",
"game-changer", "seamless", "robust", "I hope this helps!", "Great question!",
"Certainly!". No em-dash pile-ups. No paragraph opening with "Moreover," /
"Furthermore," / "Additionally,". No emoji in professional writing unless asked.

Headers should say something, not label a category — "Why students miss this", not
"Analysis".

## Safety

- **Draft by default; send only when he says "send".** Email, messages, posts are drafted
  and shown to him. When he says "send it" (or equivalent) in chat, send it, then log it in
  `wiki/send-ledger.md`. Never send on your own initiative, and never treat a request to
  draft as a request to send.
- **Never delete** files, emails, or records without explicit confirmation.
- The Google Workspace grant is broad (it includes deleting all Drive files), so the
  restraint has to live in tool permissions, not in wording. A prompt is not a permission
  layer.
- Secrets stay in `.env` and the OS keyring. Never paste a key into a note, a commit, or
  a chat.

## Tools already connected

- **Firecrawl** — CLI + 28 skills. Prefer it over MCP; the hosted MCP server was removed
  on purpose (the key would sit in plaintext in `~/.Codex.json`).
- **Google Workspace** — `gws` CLI, GCP project `ai-os-joshua`. Gmail, Calendar, Drive,
  Docs, Sheets, Slides, Tasks, People.
- **GitHub** — `gh` CLI, authenticated.

## Cost discipline

`AGENTS.md` reloads on every message, so keep this file lean. Prefer CLIs to MCP servers
(an MCP server can cost ~18k tokens per message in tool definitions). `/clear` between
unrelated tasks. Run the `handoff` skill past ~25% context rather than waiting for
auto-compact.

# Jay 2 — operating instructions for Codex (ai-os)

The canonical root is the repository directory containing this file (`C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os` on this Windows machine). Resolve paths from the repository root instead of assuming a saved Mac or Windows absolute path. This is the router: it holds pointers, not knowledge. Read it, then follow the routing map to the right file instead of searching blind. Twin for Claude Code: `CLAUDE.md`.

## Identity and mission

You are **Jay 2**, Joshua's executive assistant. This root is his EA workspace and command center. Joshua is the founder of Aspiring Attorneys and builder of LSAT U (lsatprep.study), a premium LSAT prep platform; he is the product, voice, and content authority. Your job: take operations, admin, drafting, and research off his plate so his time goes to teaching and building. Frame work as decisions and tradeoffs, not basics.

Standing duties, run from here without re-briefing: student operations (transcripts, assignments, follow-ups via `students/`), prospect and consultation correspondence (drafted in his voice, **never auto-sent unless a pre-approved template**), platform actions on lsatprep.study, session-note ingestion from Gmail/Drive, and keeping the wiki ledgers (`tasks`/`hot`/`log`) current so the next session starts oriented.

## Routing map

Paths are relative to the repository root.

| Need | Path |
|---|---|
| **Who Joshua is** (identity, preferences, contact) | `context/about-me.md` |
| **The business** (offers, money, channels, gaps) | `context/work.md` |
| **Current priorities** (the 90-day slate) | `context/priorities.md` |
| **What we decided and why** (locked decisions) | `decisions/log.md` |
| Freshest session state (hot cache) | `wiki/hot.md` |
| LLM Wiki schema (source, page, ingest/query/lint rules) | `system/schema/llm-wiki.md` |
| Master index · work ledger · dated history | `wiki/index.md` · `wiki/tasks.md` · `wiki/log.md` |
| Product ground truth (pointers to live backends) | `wiki/dashboard.md` |
| LSAT teaching knowledge | `corpus/index.md` |
| A student — profile, transcripts, work, correspondence | `students/<name>/` — start at `students/README.md` |
| Voice for anything a student or prospect reads | `wiki/teaching-voice.md` |
| Was it sent? (every outbound draft/send) | `wiki/send-ledger.md` — append-only; Gmail is authority |
| Who the students are (name, email, sessions, links) | `students/roster.generated.md` — regenerate, never hand-edit |
| Learned facts and preferences (automemory) | native store `~/.claude/projects/C--Users-Joshu-dev-ai-os/memory/` + `MEMORY.md` index |
| Skill / agent catalog | `skills/INDEX.md`, `agents/` |
| Systems Jay 2 can reach (registry) | `connections.md` — 7 data domains, mechanism/auth/freshness; read by `/audit` |
| Operator brain (how to think about automation) | `references/3ms-framework.md` — the Three Ms; walked weekly by `/level-up` |
| Automation build backlog (what to build next, ranked) | `references/automation-backlog.md` — corpus-derived gaps + tiers; feeds `/level-up` |
| How-it-works reference notes (methods, not state) | `references/` — also `references/claude-plus-codex.md`, `references/obsidian-command-center.md`, `references/second-brain-levels.md` |
| Web research and Firecrawl agents | `references/firecrawl.md` (guidelines in `references/firecrawl/`) |
| Immutable source evidence · intake queue | `raw/sources/` · `raw/inbox/` — one inbox, one archive |
| Archived web clips, with provenance + hashes | `raw/sources/clips/<slug>/` — clip + `PROVENANCE.md` + `SHA256SUMS` |
| Raw personal-data exports (Google Takeout, Gemini session transcripts) | `raw/data-about-me/` — unprocessed PII, git-ignored; never read wholesale |
| Design/plan thinking, dated (grill-me + interview outputs) | `brainstorms/` — supersedes the retired `aios/` reform folder |
| Session handoffs · chat exports | `handoffs/` — operational records, deliberately OUTSIDE `raw/`; `session-handoff` writes here |
| External teardowns and research, dated | `research/` |
| Web-clipped articles (Obsidian Web Clipper) | `raw/inbox/` — unprocessed only; `ingest` copies and hash-verifies them into `raw/sources/clips/`; processed originals stay until removal is authorized |
| Application code | `projects/lsatu/` — own repo, own instructions, own remote |
| Other projects (life-path, …) | `projects/<name>/` — each with its own `CLAUDE.md` + `.claude/` |

## Retrieval order

1. `wiki/hot.md` — current-session narrative and open threads.
2. `wiki/index.md` → the page (teaching knowledge: `corpus/index.md`; a student: their folder). Follow links; there is no semantic search and none is needed at this size.
3. The live system — the final freshness escalation.

**Live systems are authority for operational state; the brain mirrors them:** Cal.com + Google Calendar own sessions scheduled/used, LSAT U Supabase owns homework status/dossier/publish state, Stripe owns payment events, Gmail owns correspondence. On any disagreement, the backend wins. The brain is primary — nothing upstream holds them — for transcripts, teaching notes, judgments, prep briefs, curriculum, product specs, and decisions.

**Do not read the wiki unless the task needs it.** Retrieval costs context every turn. Skip it for: code edits in `projects/lsatu/`; shell/Git/file ops; questions the injected memories already answer; a skill run that names its own inputs; anything mechanical and self-contained. Route to it for: what is X · what did we decide and why · who a student is and where they stand · anything drafted in Joshua's voice for someone else · any decision touching roadmap, pedagogy, or UX.

**LLM Wiki schema:** For knowledge intake, knowledge questions, durable synthesis, and wiki maintenance, follow `system/schema/llm-wiki.md`. Use `ingest` as the single intake entry point; keep sources immutable, compile into existing pages, update the complete fenced catalog in `wiki/index.md`, and append changes to `wiki/log.md`. Preserve domain homes and live-system authority. Mechanical tasks retain the retrieval exceptions above.

**Wiki operations (LLM-wiki pattern):** the LLM writes/maintains `wiki/` and `corpus/`; Joshua sources, explores, asks. Raw sources are immutable — read, never modify. *Ingest:* read the source from `raw/`, discuss takeaways, write/update the pages it touches, update `wiki/index.md`, append to `wiki/log.md` (`## [YYYY-MM-DD] ingest | Title`); one source at a time, supervised, unless Joshua says batch. *Query:* index first, then pages; file valuable answers back as pages so explorations compound. *Lint:* `second-brain-lint` for contradictions, stale claims, orphans, missing pages.

## Voice

- **No em-dashes, ever.** Joshua never types them; a stray em-dash reads as AI and costs trust.
- **No AI-slop vocabulary** — never "delve," "tapestry," "testament," "demystify," "boasts," "in the realm of," and their kin.
- **Anything a student or prospect will read** routes through `wiki/teaching-voice.md` and is drafted, never sent, unless it is a pre-approved template.
- **When an outbound message is authorized**, preserve the draft's paragraph breaks, list lines, and intentional spacing. After sending, compare the recipient-facing rendering with the draft and confirm exactly one copy landed. Report any mismatch; never resend automatically.
- **Lead with your recommendation, not a menu.** Be decisive; don't over-hedge.
- **Any prompt Joshua will paste elsewhere** goes inside a fenced code block, never inline prose.

## Tools, keys, and secrets

- **The entire secret model is `.env` + `.gitignore`.** The root `.env` (git-ignored — verify with `git check-ignore .env`) is Joshua's single central store for **everything**: API keys, passwords, and bank/account info (decided 2026-07-17). OAuth client secrets live in `~/.config/gws/`, outside the repo. There is no vault, no Keychain, no encrypted store (`records.sparsebundle` is dead) and none is wanted. Never paste a credential into chat — add it to `.env` directly in the editor.
- **Safety is the tool layer, not prompts:** allow/deny tool lists + scoped API keys. Jay 2 acts under its own credentials and never impersonates Joshua.
- **Connected live systems:** Cal.com, Google Calendar, LSAT U Supabase, Stripe, Gmail. Full registry in `connections.md`.
- **Google access is `gws` CLI only** (`gws gmail|drive|calendar|docs …`, keyring-auth; see `skills/codex/gws-shared/`). Never the Google connector MCPs — the CLI is faster, batchable, and exports Docs to markdown.
- **Government IDs stay outside this OS.** Everything else (student names, emails, schedules, transcripts, notes, payment *links*) is ordinary local working material — classify by content, never by filename.
- **Git remote is enabled.** `origin` is GitHub (`vnjkoxpl-42905/ai-os`, decided 2026-09-29). The outer repo never tracks `.env`, `projects/lsatu/` (own repo), runtime logs, or locks. Do not create gitlinks.

When you execute it, this is what the current instructions require:

1. **Identify the session.** An explicit student, date, or transcript takes priority. Otherwise, it uses the session identified in the conversation. With no session context, it finds your most recent completed tutoring session through Calendar. Naming a student means that student’s latest completed session. It asks only if the evidence remains ambiguous.

2. **Find and read the full transcript.** It checks the student’s local folder first, then Google Calendar and Drive for “Notes by Gemini,” using `gws`. It files missing transcripts locally. If it cannot find the transcript, it reports where it looked and stops instead of inventing a lesson.

3. **Ground the teaching.** It reads your teaching voice, copy corrections, relevant corpus pages, and existing lessons. It identifies the main concept, the student’s sticking points, actual homework, and your promised follow-ups.

4. **Write a complete student-facing lesson.** This goes beyond summarizing the conversation. It includes worked examples, why the method works, tempting mistakes, practice checks with explanations, and a final transfer prompt. The canonical Markdown note lives at `students/<slug>/recaps/YYYY-MM-DD-recap.md`.

5. **Keep private notes separate.** Student weaknesses, administrative details, teaching judgments, and your follow-ups go beneath a private divider. It also updates the student’s session record and open loops.

6. **Build an interactive HTML preview.** It creates a dated folder under `brainstorms/`, using the LSAT U reading surface as the model. Expect diagrams where useful, typed practice answers, and worked feedback. Any simplified keyword-based answer checking must be disclosed.

7. **Verify and file the result.** It checks the logic, worked answers, visuals, and interactions. New designs receive desktop/mobile checks. It runs the publishing preflight in dry-run mode and logs the recap.

8. **Show you the finished draft.** You receive the preview and source paths, any limitations, and a clear statement about whether anything was posted.

**By default, it creates and files the recap but does not post, assign, email, or send it.** If you explicitly request assignment or posting, it uses the LSAT U platform workflow. That path does not involve Lovable.

It runs on demand. It does not automatically watch Calendar or run after every session. This turn renamed and inspected the skill; it did not generate a recap.

- **Root stays thin.** Don't accumulate files at the root; work products go to their homes (wiki, students, corpus, projects). Anything left at root gets filed before the session ends.
- **Delegate bulk work.** Exploration or analysis spanning 3+ files goes to a sub-agent that returns summaries, not file dumps.
- **Shell ergonomics.** Run one command per call — chained `cmd; cmd` and `rm -rf X && clone Y` forms trip permission denials that the split commands would not. Never poll with `sleep`. Use backgrounded execution for anything slow, and raise the timeout explicitly for known-slow ops (large moves, typecheck-gated pushes, full verify runs) rather than eating the default.
- **Search before creating.** One authoritative page per subject — update it, don't grow a parallel truth. `wiki/index.md` catalogs every page and updates on every ingest.
- **Preserve provenance and source hashes.** Never move, delete, or modify a migration source root — copy and hash-verify. Never follow a source symlink outside its registered root.
- **Conflicts stay explicit until adjudicated** — never silently overwrite one source generation with another.
- **Automation writes only generated files or fenced generated sections,** through compare-and-swap.
- **Obey nested instruction files** — they win over broader ones for their subtree. LSATU's recovered `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` are inviolate: never regenerate them without Joshua's explicit approval.
- **Memory = native automemory.** "Remember that…" writes one fact per file to the native store; `MEMORY.md` indexes it. This file is the rules; memory is learned facts — never mix them. Transcripts and raw captures never auto-promote.
- **Append meaningful system changes** to `wiki/log.md`; log locked decisions to `decisions/log.md`.

## Dual-runtime (Codex + Claude)

- Begin at the Git-root `AGENTS.md` and follow directory-scoped instruction files toward the working path; the nearest file wins for its subtree.
- Keep root instructions inside the runtime byte budget. Move narrow rules to the narrowest owning directory rather than growing this file.
- Activated skills are **copies** in `.agents/skills/` (from `skills/codex/`); agent definitions convert to `.codex/agents/*.toml` with the instructions in `developer_instructions`.
- Claude reads `CLAUDE.md` and never this file. Anything that must hold for both runtimes goes in BOTH files — when you change it here, mirror it there; keep the routing map and guardrails byte-identical between them.
- Activation is unequal by design: Codex reads copies in `.agents/skills/`, Claude reads copies in `.claude/skills/`. Codex and Claude both activate the LLM Wiki ingest, query, and lint workflows. Other runtime-specific activation differences remain declared in `skills/PARITY.md`. Never have separate runtimes writing the same page concurrently.
- Never have Claude and Codex editing the same file at once; pass work between them by session handoff (summarize → clear → paste). At ~250k tokens, hand off rather than riding autocompact.

The first sentence explains it in ordinary language.\\r\\n- The first example makes the distinction visible before formal symbols or combined inferences appear.\\r\\n- Each section teaches one move, asks a question, and explains the answer with a *different* example when possible.\\r\\n- Visuals do reasoning work: a changing count reveals a threshold; a group diagram reveals an overlap; a counterexample shows why a proposed inference fails.\\r\\n- The reader answers inline checks and a cumulative drill directly on the page. This is the canonical voice doc: route all student-facing and brand copy through it. Built from a grill with Joshua (2026-06-13), then tested and enriched against the full corpus of his real correspondence (944 messages he authored, mid-2025 to mid-2026, from the Gmail takeout; 2026-07-18). Claims below marked with a quote are evidenced by that corpus.\\r\\n\\r\\nIt replaces the old two-register / 15-named-tools \\"preserve verbatim\\" profile (deleted 2026-06-10) and folds in the brand/marketing register the earlier draft was missing.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Core voice (every register)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe constant under all three registers below. This is Joshua on the page.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Quiet authority.** State the value and let it land. Never oversell, never beg, never perform enthusiasm.\\r\\n- **Specific, never generic.** Real scores, the actual skill, the student\'s own history. Praise is a specific observation, not \\"great job.\\"\\r\\n- **Honest about the work, gentle about the person.** Be blunt that the LSAT is hard (\\"expect this to be exhausting and very challenging\\"). Never be blunt about a student\'s shortcomings. Honesty points at the material; warmth points at the person. When someone slips, nudge gently, never accuse.\\r\\n- **Light, grounded metaphor, understated in email.** In his real correspondence the recurring image is quiet: \\"partner with you on your LSAT journey,\\" \\"getting set up,\\" \\"foundational.\\" The vivid images (runway, climb, march toward November, an easy door to walk through) belong to authored teaching and brand copy, not to email. Keep metaphor light and grounded; never float off into abstraction.\\r\\n- **Balanced rhythm.** Short declaratives plus one slightly longer warm beat. Air between ideas. Each idea gets its own line. Real messages are short and single-purpose (median ~280 characters).\\r\\n- **Plain professional diction.** No corporate jargon, no startup hype (\\"unlock,\\" \\"crush,\\" \\"level up,\\" \\"game-changer\\" — \\"crush\\" appears once in 944 messages). Contractions are the norm, not the exception. Exclamation points are genuine, not performed: a warm message often carries one, occasionally more, especially in openers (\\"Sorry for such a long delay!\\"). He is not exclamation-averse.\\r\\n- **Forward-looking.** End on the next step or what\'s ahead.\\r\\n- **No em dashes, ever.** Use periods, colons before lists, the middot (·) as a separator, and numbered steps for procedures.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Openings, closings, and signature phrases\\r\\n\\r\\nThe mechanical fingerprint of his email, from the real corpus. Match these when drafting as Joshua.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Greeting.** \\"Hi [Name],\\" is the default (used ~519x). \\"Hey [Name],\\" for established/returning students (~229x, warmer). \\"Hello [Name],\\" (~105x) and \\"Dear [Name],\\" (~18x, formal) for first contact or a more formal note.\\r\\n- **Sign-off.** \\"Best,\\" and \\"Best regards,\\" are the workhorses (~360x / ~237x). \\"Thanks,\\" when it\'s a favor or logistics (~146x). \\"Warmly,\\" / \\"Warm regards,\\" (~54x) for a genuinely warm note. \\"Talk soon,\\" (~9x) for someone he\'ll see again soon.\\r\\n- **Signature.** Almost always signed **\\"Joshua\\"** (844 of 944 messages). The name is near-universal; include it.\\r\\n- **Signature phrases (his verbal fingerprint, use naturally, don\'t overuse):** \\"let me know\\" (by far the most common, ~390x), \\"looking forward,\\" \\"I hope\\" / \\"hope all is well\\" / \\"hope you,\\" \\"no worries at all,\\" \\"happy to\\" / \\"more than happy to,\\" \\"just wanted to make sure,\\" \\"make sure,\\" \\"no rush,\\" \\"of course.\\"\\r\\n- **Punctuation he actually uses:** semicolons (correctly, ~41x); ellipses essentially never. (For em-dashes, the hard rule in Core voice governs — never.)\\r\\n\\r\\n## The apology / accountability move\\r\\n\\r\\nOne of his most frequent and characteristic behaviors, and worth naming on its own. When he is late to reply, or missed or mishandled something, he opens by owning it plainly, often with a brief honest reason, then pivots straight to the fix. No over-apologizing, no excuses dressed up.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'m so sorry. I thought I had let you know ... I clearly didn\'t communicate that as well as I should have.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'ve been away from work for personal reasons, but I\'m back now and getting caught up.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe pattern: own it in the first line, give the real reason in one clause, move to what happens next. Warm, candid, brief.\\r\\n\\r\\n## When something on his side broke (approved shape, 2026-09-11)\\r\\n\\r\\nFrom the Sandra booking-error reply, edited by Joshua line by line over three drafts and then sent as-is. Use this shape whenever a student hit a bug or a mistake that was his. The sent text is the reference:\\r\\n\\r\\n> Hi Sandra,\\r\\n>\\r\\n> I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet. The page was showing a few times that the system then refused, and it looks like you landed on those. That is fixed now.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Your link is the same one as before:\\r\\n> [link]\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Pick any time it shows and it will book. If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Once again, my apologies.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Best,\\r\\n> Joshua\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Apology first, as the opening line.** \\"I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\" The ownership sits in the first two sentences, before any explanation.\\r\\n2. **State their position plainly, as a confirmation.** \\"To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet.\\" Answer the question they actually asked. Don\'t mention the package or credits unless the situation calls for it.\\r\\n3. **One-sentence explanation, then \\"That is fixed now.\\"** No mechanics, no system names.\\r\\n4. **Hand them the next step, plus the manual fallback.** The link, \\"pick any time it shows and it will book,\\" and the offer to do it by hand: \\"If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\"\\r\\n5. **Invite the next report:** \\"If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\"\\r\\n6. **Close with \\"Once again, my apologies.\\"** then \\"Best,\\" and \\"Joshua\\".\\r\\n\\r\\nCut from the draft, do not reuse:\\r\\n- \\"Sorry for the runaround\\" as a sign-off. The apology opens the email; it is not a closing quip.\\r\\n- \\"You will get a calendar invite with the Google Meet link right after.\\" Do not narrate what the system will send; it reads as a promise about machinery.\\r\\n- \\"You have all 10 sessions\\" / \\"nothing was used from your package.\\" Leave the package out unless it is needed; the reassurance they want is that nothing is booked, not an accounting.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Situational micro-templates\\r\\n\\r\\nVerbatim-grounded reference lines for the situations that recur most. Adapt, never paste blindly.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Student reschedules / cancels:** low-pressure, no guilt.\\r\\n  > No worries at all. It happens, so please don\'t worry about it. If you would like to reschedule, just let me know.\\r\\n- **He missed / no-showed (approved make-good template):** full ownership, real reason, offer to make it right (see the apology move above). When the cause was an unexpected health issue, the approved shape is: sincerely apologize, state that a serious health scare unexpectedly took him out of commission, offer a **completely free, full LSAT session**, and hand them the complimentary booking link `https://cal.com/joshua-jtx5ud/complimentary-session`. Emphasis stays limited: bold the complimentary offer, italicize the line that one focused session can put points on the board. Draft in Gmail; never send without Joshua\'s explicit go-ahead.\\r\\n- **Consultation reminder (day-of):**\\r\\n  > Just checking in before our consultation today. Looking forward to speaking with you. I just wanted to make sure everything is still good.\\r\\n- **Consultation follow-up:** warm, specific to their situation.\\r\\n  > Really nice meeting you. I enjoyed our conversation ... I\'m glad we got to talk through where you\'re at and what you\'re aiming for on test day.\\r\\n- **Inbound prospect (hasn\'t booked):** state availability plainly, no overselling, hand them the next step.\\r\\n  > Thanks for reaching out ... I\'d be happy to talk more about what you\'re working on and see if we\'d be a good fit. You can schedule a consultation here.\\r\\n- **Student under real-life stress:** meet the person first.\\r\\n  > Please don\'t apologize ... it sounds like you are dealing with an incredibly stressful and demanding situation.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The three registers\\r\\n\\r\\nWhich voice governs which surface.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. Coaching (earnest) -- inbox, recaps, in-drill feedback, email\\r\\n\\r\\nFully earnest. Warm, sincere, calm, patient. No jokes. The closest thing to being in the room with Joshua. Normalizes struggle, then moves to the work.\\r\\n\\r\\nReference line (target tone):\\r\\n\\r\\n> Totally normal to trip on this one. Let\'s slow down: what is the author actually concluding? Once you see it, the trap answers lose their grip. You\'ve got this.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Encouragement (student missed a hard one):** honest first, then forward. Name that it\'s genuinely hard, stay calm, move to the work. Not soft-reassuring, not cold.\\r\\n  > Missing this is expected. It\'s one of the hardest moves on the test. Let\'s slow down and see where it slipped.\\r\\n- **Accountability (student isn\'t doing the work):** gentle nudge, low pressure. Frame it as a slip, find a rhythm together. Never \\"the reps aren\'t happening,\\" never tough love.\\r\\n- **Praise (student nails it):** name the exact skill, tie it to their history, raise the bar.\\r\\n  > That\'s the cleanest you\'ve split premise from conclusion yet. Let\'s push it into the harder sets.\\r\\n- **Hard truth about the test:** state it plainly. \\"Do not expect for it to come easy. Expect to find this exhausting.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2. Teaching content (earnest substance, wit at the edges) -- bootcamp lessons, drill explanations\\r\\n\\r\\nThe substance stays earnest and clear (you are explaining a hard skill). The wit lives only at the edges: headers, openers, transitions. No jokes mid-explanation, nothing that costs comprehension.\\r\\n\\r\\n> Header: \\"The flaw hides in plain sight.\\"\\r\\n> Body: earnest, clear, step by step.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 3. Brand (sharp wit) -- landing, auth, marketing\\r\\n\\r\\nConfident and clever, the way a good lawyer is clever. Wit tied to the real skill, not wordplay for its own sake. Playful is allowed, but every clever line must be earned and true. Hollow cleverness fails (the killed \\"the next card is the page in front of you\\" was clever but empty).\\r\\n\\r\\n> Most prep teaches the test. We teach the tell.\\r\\n\\r\\nBrand copy speaks as the platform (\\"we\\", \\"you\\"), not as an individual (\\"I\\", \\"Joshua\\"). The product is the coach; no single person narrates the marketing.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Don\'t\\r\\n\\r\\n- No cold-testing or gotcha tone. (Ties to teach-first-calibrate-after.)\\r\\n- No condescension or empty cheerleading. Encouragement must sit on real substance.\\r\\n- No generic praise, no hollow cleverness, no hedging (\\"you might want to\\").\\r\\n- No hype/startup vocabulary.\\r\\n- No em dashes, ever.\\r\\n\\r\\nCorrections log: [[COPY-CORRECTIONS]] records every student-facing wording fix and\\r\\nthe reason it was wrong. Read this before\\r\\nwriting or editing copy for LSAT U so the same mistake is not made twice.\\r\\n\\r\\nCompanion to [[teaching-voice]], which says how the writing should sound. This\\r\\nsays what has actually gone wrong and why.\\r\\n\\r\\nStarted 2026-09-07 from a Read, Recall, Colour pass. Add to it every time a\\r\\ncorrection is made.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The rules these corrections came from\\r\\n\\r\\nThree rules already existed and all three leaked anyway, because each was\\r\\nenforced on the components that happened to exist when it was written. A surface\\r\\nadded later starts uncovered.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **No em dashes, ever.** [[teaching-voice]], Core voice.\\r\\n- **No internal vocabulary in student copy.** `projects/lsatu/src/features/activity-centre/CONTEXT.md`\\r\\n  carries the glossary and marks what to avoid.\\r\\n- **Every CSS token a stylesheet uses must be defined in it.** `projects/lsatu/CLAUDE.md`.\\r\\n\\r\\nGuards now live with the content rather than with each component:\\r\\n`content/instructions-voice.test.ts` checks the authored instructions, so every\\r\\nsurface that renders them is covered, including surfaces not written yet.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Corrections\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"Recall Rephrase Colour\\" → \\"Read, Recall, Colour\\"\\r\\nThe door\'s heading was hardcoded to a name the product does not have, one line\\r\\nunder a chip reading \\"Read, Recall, Colour\\". \\"Rephrase\\" belongs to a different\\r\\nActivity, Conditional Rephrase. A test asserted the wrong name, which is why\\r\\n2,600 passing tests never caught it.\\r\\n**Lesson:** when a test pins a string, check the string is right, not just that\\r\\nit matches.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"Intake only. Nothing comes back out yet…\\" → plain instruction\\r\\nClinical and abstract, and the sentence then told her to read \\"with full\\r\\nintonation\\" while step one is silent reading. The clause that made intonation\\r\\ninternal, \\"hear it naturally in your head\\", had been dropped in an earlier edit.\\r\\n**Lesson:** a word like \\"intake\\" reads as jargon. And when copy is trimmed,\\r\\ncheck what the trimmed clause was load-bearing for.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"Three beats through the stimulus\\" → \\"Three steps\\"\\r\\n\\"Beat\\" is the internal code name for one of the four method steps. The glossary\\r\\nsays students see **step**. The interface ten pixels below labelled the same four\\r\\nthings Step 1 to Step 4, so the page used two names for one thing.\\r\\n**Lesson:** never let an implementation name reach the page.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"22 pieces to read\\" → line removed\\r\\nA **piece** is one chunk, roughly a sentence, and the instructions on that same\\r\\npage use the word that way. The count was of stimuli, so \\"22 pieces\\" read as 22\\r\\nsentences.\\r\\n**Lesson:** a unit word must mean one thing per surface. Check what a word\\r\\nalready means on the page before reusing it.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"say it back\\" → \\"tell it back\\", \\"The Read\\" → \\"The Recall\\"\\r\\nThe library door still carried both retired names. \\"The Read\\" was step four\'s\\r\\nformer name and collided with step one, which is why it was renamed.\\r\\n**Lesson:** a rename is not finished until every row carries it. The door was\\r\\nstale for months because it is a different database row from the sections.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"then a fourth\\" → \\"then a fourth step\\"\\r\\nThe noun sat three words back and the reader had to carry it.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"once you have got all of it\\" → \\"once you have read all of it\\"\\r\\nAmbiguous between having read it and having remembered it, in the one clause\\r\\nthat triggers step four.\\r\\n**Lesson:** precision matters most where the sentence is an instruction.\\r\\n\\r\\n### The three-fact notice → one fact\\r\\n\\"Nothing is recording yet, the microphone opens on Start, and the section\\r\\nrecords in one take that you cannot pause.\\" Two of those are said again in step\\r\\nfour and in the long version, so she skipped the paragraph.\\r\\n**Lesson:** say it once, in the place it matters.\\r\\n\\r\\n### The method, told twice → the long version collapsed\\r\\nThe page rendered four numbered steps and then the whole written briefing saying\\r\\nthe same thing at length, both open. She read the method twice and could not\\r\\ntell which one to follow.\\r\\n**Lesson:** two explanations of one thing is worse than either alone.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"PT105.S1 · 24 stimuli · about 25 min\\" → removed\\r\\nThe section was already the second line of the title. The clock is at the foot\\r\\nand in the long version. The stimulus count measured the work in a unit she has\\r\\nno feel for.\\r\\n**Lesson:** delete a line that repeats what is above it. Do not reword it.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Booking emails: hand over the link, not the pass settings (2026-09-08)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Cut:** \\"70 minutes each, and no expiration date, so there\'s no rush to use them.\\"\\r\\n**Keep:** \\"You\'re set up on LSAT U with 10 sessions.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\nSession length and expiry are admin fields. The student sees them on the booking\\r\\npage when she picks a time, so putting them in the email is detail she did not ask\\r\\nfor and has to read past to reach the link. The credit count is worth saying because\\r\\nit tells her how much she has. Everything else about the pass stays in the backend.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Lesson:** in a booking email, say who it\'s for, how many sessions, and the link.\\r\\nStop there.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Drill hub: say what the button does, not what the feature is called (2026-09-09)\\r\\n\\r\\nSix changes on `/classroom/drill`, from the run-3 pass. The hub named its own\\r\\nfeatures, and it assumed the student had rejected something.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Was | Now |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| \\"Start Smart Drill\\" | \\"Practice your weakest types\\" |\\r\\n| \\"Start One Passage\\" | \\"Read one passage\\" |\\r\\n| \\"Start a Smart Drill instead\\" | \\"Or practice your weakest types\\" |\\r\\n| \\"Read one passage instead\\" | \\"Or read one passage now\\" |\\r\\n| \\"Open analytics\\" | \\"See where you lose points\\" |\\r\\n| \\"Open journal\\" | \\"Review your missed questions\\" |\\r\\n\\r\\n\\"Smart Drill\\" is the product\'s internal name for the adaptive set. On a button it\\r\\nasks the student to guess what she is about to get. The sentence above the button\\r\\nstill names it, which is where a product name belongs: after the thing has been\\r\\nexplained, not as the explanation.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\"Instead\\" was the worse one. It tells the student she has just declined the\\r\\nassigned work by reading past it. She has not. \\"Or\\" offers a second path without\\r\\nnarrating a decision she never made.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\"Open analytics\\" and \\"Open journal\\" name a screen. Internal names may stay in code, never on the page.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Never | Use instead |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| beat, beats | step |\\r\\n| chunk | piece |\\r\\n| intake | plain instruction |\\r\\n| briefing, phase, tab, card | the thing\'s own name |\\r\\n| say it back | tell it back |\\r\\n| The Read | The Recall |\\r\\n| Recall Rephrase Colour | Read, Recall, Colour |\\r\\n| em dash, en dash | a full stop, or a colon before a list |\\r\\n\\r\\n## Conditional Rephrase: name the student action, not the internal model (2026-09-15)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Cut:** “record the route,” “choose the route,” and a map presented as five rules.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Keep:** diagram the statement on paper, choose the matching diagram, and organize\\r\\nthe map into four groups. “Required means right” is a separate takeaway because it\\r\\nexplains placement; it is not a fifth group.\\r\\n\\r\\n“Route” described the system’s representation, not the student’s work. Calling five\\r\\nunlike ideas rules also flattened the teaching structure and made the layout harder to\\r\\nread.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Lesson:** name the action the student can see herself doing. Do not force a teaching\\r\\nreminder into the same hierarchy as the categories it explains.\\r\\n\\r\\nRelated: [[teaching-voice]] · [[ASSIGN-AN-ACTIVITY]] · [[STUDENT-PLATFORM-IDENTITY-MAP]]\\r\\n\\r\\n## Session recaps: write a reusable reference, not a play-by-play (2026-09-12)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Cut:** an opener saying the student got two questions right, followed by a summary of\\r\\nwhich answer they chose and how they explained it.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Keep:** the concept the student needs tomorrow, a visual model of the reasoning, a\\r\\nshort diagnostic check, and the exact practice they need to complete.\\r\\n\\r\\nA student will not remember an isolated answer-choice exchange a day later, and the\\r\\nexchange is not useful unless it demonstrates a reusable rule. Praise belongs only when it identifies a\\r\\ndurable skill or meaningful change, not merely that an answer was correct.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Lesson:** organize the recap around what the student can use next. Lead with the\\r\\nconcept, show the logic clearly, and finish with tangible practice.\\r\\n\\r\\n### A rule is not a fact (2026-09-12)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Cut:** describing a conditional Must Be True lesson as “applying a rule to a fact”\\r\\nwithout checking whether the stimulus supplied a fact at all.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Keep:** a fact is an asserted true case or condition. Never\\r\\ninvent a fact to make a rule fire.\\r\\n\\r\\n### A post-session note is lecture material, not an email (2026-09-12)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Cut:** a greeting, a dated recap heading, references to a question the student is\\r\\nexpected to remember, and a sign-off.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Keep:** a concept title, a clear opening distinction, numbered procedures, spaced\\r\\nexamples, and practice that uses the lesson.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Lesson:** the note should remain useful when the session itself is no longer fresh.\\r\\nIt must teach from the page instead of relying on remembered context.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe concept should not arrive as an abrupt list. A strong note:\\r\\n\\r\\n- reads as lecture notes, not an email or a transcript summary;\\r\\n- opens directly with the governing concept;\\r\\n- separates ideas with descriptive headings and generous spacing;\\r\\n- defines the important distinction before asking the student to use it;\\r\\n- turns Joshua\'s explanation into a reusable method;\\r\\n- uses compact tables, numbered steps, and diagrams only when they reduce cognitive load;\\r\\n- includes valid moves, invalid moves, boundary cases, and a way to test the answer;\\r\\n- gives examples that stand alone without requiring memory of a question from days ago;\\r\\n- ends with concrete practice supported by the session; and\\r\\n- keeps private teaching judgments below the `Notes for me (not posted)` divider.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Reference structure\\r\\n\\r\\nThe Sofia note uses this content-shaped progression:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Concept title.** `Conditional Must Be True: Facts, Rules, and Bridges`\\r\\n2. **Direct orientation.** The two moves are stated immediately: connect rules or use a\\r\\n   fact to activate a rule.\\r\\n3. **Method at a glance.** A small table distinguishes chaining from triggering.\\r\\n4. **Foundational distinction.** Facts and rules are defined before either is applied.\\r\\n5. **First method.** Chaining is taught through a definition, positional test, diagram,\\r\\n   valid example, invalid example, hidden case, and longer-chain consequence.\\r\\n6. **Second method.** Triggering is taught through its two legal moves and the two facts\\r\\n   that produce no inference.\\r\\n7. **Decision aid.** A four-row table makes valid and invalid directions visible.\\r\\n8. **Execution advice.** The student learns when to contrapose, when to diagram, and how\\r\\n   to test a conditional answer from its trigger.\\r\\n9. **Repeatable process.** A numbered procedure turns the lesson into something usable\\r\\n   on the next question.\\r\\n10. **Practice.** Checkboxes state the work actually assigned.\\r\\n11. **Private continuation.** Weak spots, Joshua\'s follow-ups, and teaching judgments are\\r\\n    separated from the student-facing note.\\r\\n\\r\\n## What to copy and what to vary\\r\\n\\r\\nCopy the depth, hierarchy, and independence from remembered question context. Vary the\\r\\nsections to fit the lesson. Do not force every recap into the same headings. A causation\\r\\nsession, an RC mapping session, and a conditional-logic session should not look identical.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe note is complete when the student can return several days later and use it to solve\\r\\nthe same kind of problem without reconstructing the original session.\\r\\n"}}'}]

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 3.3 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Warning: truncated output (original token count: 10535)\nTotal output lines: 2\n\n{"chunk_id":"9d5344","wall_time_seconds":1.4651424,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":3523,"output":"---\\r\\ntitle: Conditional Must Be True · Keep the Whole Statement\\r\\ntype: recap\\r\\nrecord_kind: primary\\r\\nstudent: yahunatan-zetvy\\r\\nsession_date: 2026-09-16\\r\\nsource: transcript-downloads/2026-09-16-yahunatan-zetvy-notes-by-gemini.md\\r\\nstatus: draft\\r\\nposted: false\\r\\nposted_at:\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Conditional Must Be True: Keep the Whole Statement\\r\\n\\r\\nOnly people willing to compromise should undergo mediation. This tells you what is required for mediation to be appropriate. It does not tell you who actually attends, or whether willingness alone is enough. Keeping those distinctions intact is the work of conditional reasoning.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Combine what the statements guarantee\\r\\n\\r\\nA Must Be True answer must follow from the information you were given. Sometimes you combine facts. Sometimes you connect rules. Identify what each sentence gives you before choosing a method.\\r\\n\\r\\nSuppose one type of flavonoid found in apples is an antioxidant, and antioxidants help prevent heart disease. You can conclude that at least one type of flavonoid found in apples helps prevent heart disease.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhy at least one? The first statement identifies one type with the relevant property. The second tells you what that property does. Together they support a claim about that type. They do not show that every flavonoid has the property, or that eating any apple prevents heart disease.\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep the strength of the conclusion equal to the strength of the evidence. Helps prevent does not mean always prevents.\\r\\n\\r\\nA rule works differently. If a person should undergo mediation, that person is willing to compromise tells you a relationship. It does not tell you that anyone actually should undergo mediation. A rule does not establish its own starting condition.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Check your reasoning\\r\\n\\r\\nAn apple flavonoid is an antioxidant, and antioxidants help prevent heart disease. Can you conclude that every apple flavonoid prevents heart disease? Explain.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Worked answer:** No. The evidence establishes the relevant property for at least one type, not every type. It says helps prevent, not always prevents. A second type without that property would fit the evidence and defeat the stronger answer.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Put the requirement on the right\\r\\n\\r\\nConsider this hypothetical rule: Only people willing to compromise should undergo mediation to resolve their conflict.\\r\\n\\r\\nMediation means trying to resolve a dispute with help from a neutral person. The rule limits who should use it. Willingness to compromise is required.\\r\\n\\r\\nFirst flatten the sentence into complete English:\\r\\n\\r\\nIf a person should undergo mediation, then that person is willing to compromise.\\r\\n\\r\\nNow abbreviate the complete ideas:\\r\\n\\r\\nM = the person should undergo mediation.\\r\\n\\r\\nW = the person is willing to compromise.\\r\\n\\r\\nM → W\\r\\n\\r\\nThe left side is sufficient: knowing M lets you conclude W. The right side is necessary: M cannot be true without W. Necessary does not mean enough by itself. A person can meet a requirement without qualifying for the activity.\\r\\n\\r\\nOnly if works the same way. Litigation should be pursued only if a person is sure their position is correct becomes: If the person should pursue litigation, then the person is sure their position is correct.\\r\\n\\r\\nL = the person should pursue litigation. C = the person is sure their position is correct.\\r\\n\\r\\nL → C\\r\\n\\r\\nBeing sure is required. It does not establish that the person should litigate. Also, being sure that a position is correct is not the same as the position actually being correct.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Check your reasoning\\r\\n\\r\\nOnly trained volunteers should lead the workshop. Write the complete if-then rule. Does training alone prove that a volunteer should lead?\\r\\n\\r\\n**Worked answer:** If a volunteer should lead the workshop, then that volunteer is trained. Training is required, but training alone does not prove the person should lead. Other considerations may matter. Reversing the rule would add a guarantee we were never given.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Keep should in the statement\\r\\n\\r\\nA recommendation and an action are different ideas. A person may do something they should not do. A person may also fail to do something they should do.\\r\\n\\r\\nM → W is about who should undergo mediation. It is not a rule about everyone who actually undergoes mediation.\\r\\n\\r\\nSuppose Alex actually attends mediation but refuses to compromise. That does not contradict this rule. Alex may be doing something Alex should not do. But if we say Alex should undergo mediation and Alex is unwilling to compromise, those two claims violate the rule.\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep words such as should, can, must, and actually when you translate. Removing one can change what the statement proves. An abbreviation saves writing only when you remember the whole idea behind it.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Check your reasoning\\r\\n\\r\\nWe know only that Morgan actually underwent mediation. Does the rule prove that Morgan was willing to compromise? Why?\\r\\n\\r\\n**Worked answer:** No. The rule starts with should undergo mediation, not actually underwent mediation. Morgan could have attended despite being unwilling. The actual action does not activate this recommendation rule.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Reverse and negate to get the contrapositive\\r\\n\\r\\nThe rule M → W forbids one combination: M true with W false. If willingness is absent, the recommendation cannot be present.\\r\\n\\r\\nM → W\\r\\n\\r\\nnot W → not M\\r\\n\\r\\nIn English: If a person is unwilling to compromise, then that person should not undergo mediation.\\r\\n\\r\\nYou reverse the order and negate both complete ideas. The new statement describes the same restriction as the original. This is why it is valid.\\r\\n\\r\\nReversing without negating does something different: W → M. It says willingness guarantees that mediation is appropriate. The original rule never promised that. A willing person might have a conflict for which mediation is inappropriate for another reason.\\r\\n\\r\\nNegating without reversing is also invalid: not M → not W. A person who should not undergo mediation could still be willing to compromise.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe rule lets you move forward from M, or backward from not W. W alone and not M alone leave the other side open.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Test every possible combination\\r\\n\\r\\n| Should undergo mediation | Willing to compromise | Fits M → W? |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| True | True | Yes |\\r\\n| True | False | No |\\r\\n| False | True | Yes |\\r\\n| False | False | Yes |\\r\\n\\r\\nOnly M true with W false violates the rule. Both states with M false are allowed. Both states with W true are allowed.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Check your reasoning\\r\\n\\r\\nA volunteer is not trained. What follows from the workshop rule? What if the volunteer is trained instead?\\r\\n\\r\\n**Worked answer:** The untrained volunteer should not lead the workshop. That is the contrapositive: not trained → should not lead. A trained volunteer may or may not be someone who should lead. Affirming the requirement does not establish the trigger.\\r\\n\\r\\n## A statement about a whole group can be a rule\\r\\n\\r\\nSuppose a stimulus says: People whose conflicts are based on ideology are unwilling to compromise.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn this hypothetical stimulus, the statement applies to every person in the specified group. It is not a claim about all people, and it is not a general claim you should import into other questions.\\r\\n\\r\\nI = the person’s conflict is based on ideology.\\r\\n\\r\\nI → not W\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is a conditional relationship even without the word if. If a person belongs to the named group, the description applies to that person. It does not establish that any particular person belongs to that group.\\r\\n\\r\\nNow connect it to the contrapositive:\\r\\n\\r\\nI → not W → not M\\r\\n\\r\\nTherefore: People whose conflicts are based on ideology should not undergo mediation.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe middle idea matches exactly. The group rule gets you to unwilling to compromise. The contrapositive takes you from unwilling to compromise to should not undergo mediation.\\r\\n\\r\\nIf the stimulus also says Lena’s conflict is based on ideology, that fact activates the chain. You can then conclude that Lena is unwilling to compromise and should not undergo mediation. Without that fact, your conclusion remains a rule about the group.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Check your reasoning\\r\\n\\r\\nUse I → not W and M → W. What must follow for anyone whose conflict is based on ideology? Does that prove someone actually has such a conflict?\\r\\n\\r\\n**Worked answer:** I → not M. Contrapose M → W to get not W → not M, then connect I → not W → not M. The conclusion is should not undergo mediation. The group rule does not establish that a member of that group actually exists.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Do not invent a choice between two activities\\r\\n\\r\\nThe separate rule L → C gives a requirement for litigation. It does not connect litigation to mediation.\\r\\n\\r\\nSomeone who should not undergo mediation does not automatically become someone who should pursue litigation. The stimulus has not said those are the only choices, or that every person must choose one.\\r\\n\\r\\nA counterexample makes the gap visible. Imagine a person who should use neither activity. That can fit both rules: the person does not have to meet the requirements for an activity they should not pursue.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe two requirements do not create an either-or choice. You need an additional statement connecting the activities before moving from one to the other.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Check your reasoning\\r\\n\\r\\nIf a person should not undergo mediation, must that person pursue litigation instead? Use a counterexample.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Worked answer:** No. The person could appropriately pursue neither activity. That violates neither requirement. The premises do not say that mediation and litigation are exhaustive choices, or that rejecting one requires the other.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Use the same process on a new question\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Identify what each sentence supplies: a specific fact or a general relationship.\\r\\n2. Translate each relationship into a complete if-then sentence. Preserve the subject, negation, and words such as should.\\r\\n3. Name the complete ideas before abbreviating. Put the required condition on the right.\\r\\n4. If you need the opposite direction, reverse and negate both ideas.\\r\\n5. Connect rules only when the ending of one matches the beginning of the next. Apply a fact only when it supplies a valid starting point.\\r\\n6. Read the result back in English. Test a tempting answer by trying to make the premises true and that answer false.\\r\\n\\r\\nIf you can build that counterexample, the answer is not guaranteed. If you cannot see a valid connection yet, do not add a fact or an extra choice to make the answer work.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Put the moves together\\r\\n\\r\\n1. A file may be released only if it has been reviewed. This file has not been reviewed. What follows?\\r\\n\\r\\n**Worked answer:** This file may not be released. May be released → reviewed; not reviewed → may not be released. Preserve permission: this does not prove that nobody actually releases it.\\r\\n\\r\\n2. Only licensed drivers may operate these vans. Sam is licensed. Must Sam be permitted to operate one?\\r\\n\\r\\n**Worked answer:** No. May operate → licensed. Licensing is necessary, but could be insufficient. Sam could be licensed and still lack permission for another reason.\\r\\n\\r\\n3. Every priority application needs supervisor approval. Approval is required only if the application is incomplete. What follows for priority applications?\\r\\n\\r\\n**Worked answer:** Priority → needs approval → incomplete. Every priority application is incomplete under these hypothetical rules. No particular priority application is asserted to exist.\\r\\n\\r\\nTransfer question: Only certified guides should lead night tours. All new guides are uncertified. Nora is a new guide. State the inference and one tempting answer that goes too far.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Worked answer:** New → not certified; should lead → certified; not certified → should not lead. Nora should not lead night tours. Nora never actually leads night tours goes too far: the rules concern who should lead, not what someone actually does.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Before the next session\\r\\n\\r\\nComplete the conditional-diagramming drills first, then move into the LSAT questions. The focus is translating and diagramming conditionals until the move becomes automatic.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe drills and questions are the work planned for this sequence. This note does not establish that they have already been delivered.\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## Notes for me (not posted)\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Weak spots:** complete English before symbols; sufficient versus necessary direction; retaining should versus actual action; recognizing a universal group statement as a conditional rule.\\r\\n- **Follow-ups on my side:** Joshua promised conditional-diagramming drills, followed by LSAT questions (00:18:05–00:19:25, repeated at the close). Delivery is unverified. No question IDs, drill quantity, or deadline was specified.\\r\\n- **Watch:** Yahunatan found the required compromise condition and used the contrapositive. The next target is precise rephrasing that preserves modality, followed by automatic diagramming.\\r\\n- **Source conflict:** at 00:13:57 the transcript reads willing for the ideology group; at 00:16:23 and 00:17:13 both speakers clearly use unwilling/not willing. This draft follows the repeated negated reading. The original test stimulus is not attached, so exact original wording remains unverified.\\r\\n- **Source conflict:** the current teaching-notes shorthand says would not undergo mediation. The instruction at 00:11:52–00:12:58 explicitly distinguishes should from what people actually do. The draft preserves should not undergo; it does not silently reproduce that stronger action claim.\\r\\n- **Excluded:** travel and theological conversation remain in the source. No personal or religious claims appear in the student lesson. The ideological rule is labelled hypothetical, not a real-world characterization.\\r\\n- **Preview:** [[../../../brainstorms/2026-09-30-yahunatan-post-session-recap/conditional-reasoning.html]]\\r\\n- **Source map:** [[../../../brainstorms/2026-09-30-yahunatan-post-session-recap/source-map.md]]\\r\\n- **Related reference:** [[../../sofia/recaps/2026-09-11-recap]]; corpus Conditional Logic/Notes/_megadoc_notes_conditionals.md. class=\\"dateline\\"><time datetime=\\"2026-09-16\\">2026-09-16</time></div><h1>Conditional Must Be True: Keep the Whole Statement</h1><p class=\\"lead\\">Only people willing to compromise should undergo mediation. This tells you what is required for mediation to be appropriate. It does not tell you who actually attends, or whether willingness alone is enough. Keeping those distinctions intact is the work of conditional reasoning.</p><section class=\\"chapter\\" id=\\"part-1\\"><h2>Combine what the statements guarantee</h2><p>A Must Be True answer must follow from the information you were given. Sometimes you combine facts. Sometimes you connect rules. Identify what each sentence gives you before choosing a method.</p><p>Suppose one type of flavonoid found in apples is an antioxidant, and antioxidants help prevent heart disease. You can conclude that at least one type of flavonoid found in apples helps prevent heart disease.</p><p>Why at least one? The first statement identifies one type with the relevant property. The second tells you what that property does. Together they support a claim about that type. They do not show that every flavonoid has the property, or that eating any apple prevents heart disease.</p><p>Keep the strength of the conclusion equal to the strength of the evidence. Helps prevent does not mean alwa…535 tokens truncated…the person is willing to compromise.</p><p class=\\"formula\\">M → W</p><p>The left side is sufficient: knowing M lets you conclude W. The right side is necessary: M cannot be true without W. Necessary does not mean enough by itself. A person can meet a requirement without qualifying for the activity.</p><p>Only if works the same way. Litigation should be pursued only if a person is sure their position is correct becomes: If the person should pursue litigation, then the person is sure their position is correct.</p><p>L = the person should pursue litigation. C = the person is sure their position is correct.</p><p class=\\"formula\\">L → C</p><p>Being sure is required. It does not establish that the person should litigate. Also, being sure that a position is correct is not the same as the position actually being correct.</p><section class=\\"check\\"><form><label for=\\"answer-2\\">Only trained volunteers should lead the workshop. Write the complete if-then rule. Does training alone prove that a volunteer should lead?</label><textarea id=\\"answer-2\\" rows=\\"3\\" required placeholder=\\"Write your answer and explain why.\\"></textarea><button type=\\"submit\\">Check my answer</button></form><div class=\\"feedback\\" hidden tabindex=\\"-1\\"><strong>Compare your reasoning</strong><p>If a volunteer should lead the workshop, then that volunteer is trained. Training is required, but training alone does not prove the person should lead. Other considerations may matter. Reversing the rule would add a guarantee we were never given.</p><p class=\\"small\\">Your response stays above. Check whether it preserves the direction, the negation, and the strength of the claim. This exercise does not automatically grade your reasoning.</p><button class=\\"again\\" type=\\"button\\">Try again</button></div><noscript><p><strong>Worked answer:</strong> If a volunteer should lead the workshop, then that volunteer is trained. Training is required, but training alone does not prove the person should lead. Other considerations may matter. Reversing the rule would add a guarantee we were never given.</p></noscript></section></section><section class=\\"chapter\\" id=\\"part-3\\"><h2>Keep should in the statement</h2><p>A recommendation and an action are different ideas. A person may do something they should not do. A person may also fail to do something they should do.</p><p>M → W is about who should undergo mediation. It is not a rule about everyone who actually undergoes mediation.</p><p>Suppose Alex actually attends mediation but refuses to compromise. That does not contradict this rule. Alex may be doing something Alex should not do. But if we say Alex should undergo mediation and Alex is unwilling to compromise, those two claims violate the rule.</p><p>Keep words such as should, can, must, and actually when you translate. Removing one can change what the statement proves. An abbreviation saves writing only when you remember the whole idea behind it.</p><section class=\\"check\\"><form><label for=\\"answer-3\\">We know only that Morgan actually underwent mediation. Does the rule prove that Morgan was willing to compromise? Why?</label><textarea id=\\"answer-3\\" rows=\\"3\\" required placeholder=\\"Write your answer and explain why.\\"></textarea><button type=\\"submit\\">Check my answer</button></form><div class=\\"feedback\\" hidden tabindex=\\"-1\\"><strong>Compare your reasoning</strong><p>No. The rule starts with should undergo mediation, not actually underwent mediation. Morgan could have attended despite being unwilling. The actual action does not activate this recommendation rule.</p><p class=\\"small\\">Your response stays above. Check whether it preserves the direction, the negation, and the strength of the claim. This exercise does not automatically grade your reasoning.</p><button class=\\"again\\" type=\\"button\\">Try again</button></div><noscript><p><strong>Worked answer:</strong> No. The rule starts with should undergo mediation, not actually underwent mediation. Morgan could have attended despite being unwilling. The actual action does not activate this recommendation rule.</p></noscript></section></section><section class=\\"chapter\\" id=\\"part-4\\"><h2>Reverse and negate to get the contrapositive</h2><p>The rule M → W forbids one combination: M true with W false. If willingness is absent, the recommendation cannot be present.</p><p class=\\"formula\\">M → W</p><p class=\\"formula\\">not W → not M</p><p>In English: If a person is unwilling to compromise, then that person should not undergo mediation.</p><p>You reverse the order and negate both complete ideas. The new statement describes the same restriction as the original. This is why it is valid.</p><p>Reversing without negating does something different: W → M. It says willingness guarantees that mediation is appropriate. The original rule never promised that. A willing person might have a conflict for which mediation is inappropriate for another reason.</p><p>Negating without reversing is also invalid: not M → not W. A person who should not undergo mediation could still be willing to compromise.</p><p>The rule lets you move forward from M, or backward from not W. W alone and not M alone leave the other side open.</p><section class=\\"model\\" aria-labelledby=\\"model-title\\"><h3 id=\\"model-title\\">Which combination breaks the rule?</h3><p>Change the two claims for one hypothetical person. M means should undergo mediation. W means willing to compromise. These switches describe a test case under the stated rule.</p><fieldset><legend>Choose a case</legend><label><input id=\\"m\\" type=\\"checkbox\\" checked> M: should undergo mediation</label><label><input id=\\"w\\" type=\\"checkbox\\" checked> W: willing to compromise</label></fieldset><div id=\\"case-result\\" role=\\"status\\" aria-live=\\"polite\\"></div><table><caption>All four combinations under M → W</caption><thead><tr><th scope=\\"col\\">M</th><th scope=\\"col\\">W</th><th scope=\\"col\\">Fits the rule?</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr data-m=\\"1\\" data-w=\\"1\\"><td>True</td><td>True</td><td>Yes</td></tr><tr data-m=\\"1\\" data-w=\\"0\\"><td>True</td><td>False</td><td>No: required W is missing</td></tr><tr data-m=\\"0\\" data-w=\\"1\\"><td>False</td><td>True</td><td>Yes</td></tr><tr data-m=\\"0\\" data-w=\\"0\\"><td>False</td><td>False</td><td>Yes</td></tr></tbody></table><p class=\\"small\\">Both cases with M false fit the rule. That is why not M tells you nothing about W. Both cases with W true fit it. That is why W does not establish M.</p></section><section class=\\"check\\"><form><label for=\\"answer-4\\">A volunteer is not trained. What follows from the workshop rule? What if the volunteer is trained instead?</label><textarea id=\\"answer-4\\" rows=\\"3\\" required placeholder=\\"Write your answer and explain why.\\"></textarea><button type=\\"submit\\">Check my answer</button></form><div class=\\"feedback\\" hidden tabindex=\\"-1\\"><strong>Compare your reasoning</strong><p>The untrained volunteer should not lead the workshop. That is the contrapositive: not trained → should not lead. A trained volunteer may or may not be someone who should lead. Affirming the requirement does not establish the trigger.</p><p class=\\"small\\">Your response stays above. Check whether it preserves the direction, the negation, and the strength of the claim. This exercise does not automatically grade your reasoning.</p><button class=\\"again\\" type=\\"button\\">Try again</button></div><noscript><p><strong>Worked answer:</strong> The untrained volunteer should not lead the workshop. That is the contrapositive: not trained → should not lead. A trained volunteer may or may not be someone who should lead. Affirming the requirement does not establish the trigger.</p></noscript></section></section><section class=\\"chapter\\" id=\\"part-5\\"><h2>A statement about a whole group can be a rule</h2><p>Suppose a stimulus says: People whose conflicts are based on ideology are unwilling to compromise.</p><p>In this hypothetical stimulus, the statement applies to every person in the specified group. It is not a claim about all people, and it is not a general claim you should import into other questions.</p><p>I = the person’s conflict is based on ideology.</p><p class=\\"formula\\">I → not W</p><p>This is a conditional relationship even without the word if. If a person belongs to the named group, the description applies to that person. It does not establish that any particular person belongs to that group.</p><p>Now connect it to the contrapositive:</p><p class=\\"formula\\">I → not W → not M</p><p>Therefore: People whose conflicts are based on ideology should not undergo mediation.</p><p>The middle idea matches exactly. The group rule gets you to unwilling to compromise. The contrapositive takes you from unwilling to compromise to should not undergo mediation.</p><p>If the stimulus also says Lena’s conflict is based on ideology, that fact activates the chain. You can then conclude that Lena is unwilling to compromise and should not undergo mediation. Without that fact, your conclusion remains a rule about the group.</p><section class=\\"check\\"><form><label for=\\"answer-5\\">Use I → not W and M → W. What must follow for anyone whose conflict is based on ideology? Does that prove someone actually has such a conflict?</label><textarea id=\\"answer-5\\" rows=\\"3\\" required placeholder=\\"Write your answer and explain why.\\"></textarea><button type=\\"submit\\">Check my answer</button></form><div class=\\"feedback\\" hidden tabindex=\\"-1\\"><strong>Compare your reasoning</strong><p>I → not M. Contrapose M → W to get not W → not M, then connect I → not W → not M. The conclusion is should not undergo mediation. The group rule does not establish that a member of that group actually exists.</p><p class=\\"small\\">Your response stays above. Check whether it preserves the direction, the negation, and the strength of the claim. This exercise does not automatically grade your reasoning.</p><button class=\\"again\\" type=\\"button\\">Try again</button></div><noscript><p><strong>Worked answer:</strong> I → not M. Contrapose M → W to get not W → not M, then connect I → not W → not M. The conclusion is should not undergo mediation. The group rule does not establish that a member of that group actually exists.</p></noscript></section></section><section class=\\"chapter\\" id=\\"part-6\\"><h2>Do not invent a choice between two activities</h2><p>The separate rule L → C gives a requirement for litigation. It does not connect litigation to mediation.</p><p>Someone who should not undergo mediation does not automatically become someone who should pursue litigation. The stimulus has not said those are the only choices, or that every person must choose one.</p><p>A counterexample makes the gap visible. Imagine a person who should use neither activity. That can fit both rules: the person does not have to meet the requirements for an activity they should not pursue.</p><p>The two requirements do not create an either-or choice. You need an additional statement connecting the activities before moving from one to the other.</p><section class=\\"check\\"><form><label for=\\"answer-6\\">If a person should not undergo mediation, must that person pursue litigation instead?
