It covers source retrieval, the primary student record, and private follow-ups. A request only to find or inspect a transcript stops at that narrower task.\\r\\n\\r\\nAfter every session Joshua wants a durable set of lecture notes. The student should be\\r\\nable to return several days later, understand the lesson without remembering a specific\\r\\nquestion, and apply the method to new work. It is teaching content, not an email or a\\r\\nsession summary.\\r\\n\\r\\nRead `skills/reference/session-recap-quality-reference.md` before drafting. Its Sofia\\r\\nnote is the quality bar for depth, hierarchy, nuance, and practical usefulness. Copy the\\r\\nmethod, not the conditional-logic headings.\\r\\n\\r\\nDraft and file the note by default. If Joshua explicitly says to post, assign, publish,\\r\\nor send it to the student, complete that as a separate LSAT U platform action after the\\r\\ndraft is ready and verify what landed. Never infer posting permission from a request to\\r\\nwrite a note.\\r\\n\\r\\n## 1. Get the transcript on disk first\\r\\n\\r\\nTranscripts come from Google Meet\'s Gemini notes. The calendar event carries the Drive\\r\\ndoc as an attachment; some sessions have the doc in Drive but never got it attached.\\r\\nCheck both.\\r\\n\\r\\nUse `gws calendar events list` on the primary calendar for the date window. Match the student\'s guest email, never just the event title. Then use `gws drive files list` for native Docs whose name contains `Notes by Gemini` in the same window. Include unattached Docs and untitled events named `Meeting started ...`. Export each matching native Doc with `gws drive files export` and MIME type `text/plain`; Markdown export expands and escapes the transcript. Build the command\'s JSON `--params` argument for the active shell rather than copying Bash quoting into PowerShell.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe Drive result can include Markdown copies uploaded by an earlier intake. Count native\\r\\nGoogle Docs as source transcripts and use the file ID to deduplicate. Do not count an\\r\\nuploaded `YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>-notes-by-gemini.md` copy as another session. Reconcile the\\r\\nfull week against Calendar before exporting so unattached docs and events with no doc\\r\\nboth remain visible in the report.\\r\\n\\r\\nFile to `students/<slug>/transcript-downloads/YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>-notes-by-gemini.md`.\\r\\nResolve the person with `students/_aliases.md`; for a \\"Meeting started\\" doc, count\\r\\nspeaker labels in the transcript (use `rg -o \\"^[A-Z][a-z]+( [A-Z][a-z]+)?:\\"` and count the labels).\\r\\nConsultations and people without a folder go to `students/_other-sessions/`.\\r\\n**Never create a student folder without asking.** Skip anything already on disk.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe Google Classroom calendars (`c_classroom...`) have been empty since 2026; the\\r\\nprimary calendar holds every session.\\r\\n\\r\\n## 2. Read the whole transcript, not the Gemini summary\\r\\n\\r\\nThe Gemini \\"Quick notes\\" flatten what he said. Read the transcript section. It is 40\\r\\nto 90 KB; that is the cost of a recap that is true.\\r\\n\\r\\nExtract:\\r\\n\\r\\n- the governing concept and distinctions Joshua taught;\\r\\n- the student\'s actual confusion or decision point;\\r\\n- the reasoning procedure, including why each step works;\\r\\n- legal and illegal moves, edge cases, diagnostic checks, and shortcuts;\\r\\n- examples that can stand alone outside the original question; and\\r\\n- the exact practice and follow-ups that were assigned.\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not write a play-by-play of answer choices. A detail from a specific question belongs\\r\\nonly when it demonstrates a reusable move. If the explanation needs more support, search\\r\\nJoshua\'s corpus first. Use an authoritative outside source only when Joshua points to it\\r\\nor the corpus cannot resolve the concept. Keep source research outside the student note.\\r\\nThe session transcript remains the authority for what happened and what was assigned.\\r\\n\\r\\n## 3. Write the recap\\r\\n\\r\\nPath: `students/<slug>/recaps/YYYY-MM-DD-recap.md`. One file per session. Primary\\r\\nrecord: never regenerate over an existing one; a redo gets a dated correction section.\\r\\n\\r\\n```markdown\\r\\n---\\r\\ntitle: Recap · <Student> · YYYY-MM-DD\\r\\ntype: recap\\r\\nrecord_kind: primary\\r\\nstudent: <slug>\\r\\nsession_date: YYYY-MM-DD\\r\\nsource: transcript-downloads/YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>-notes-by-gemini.md\\r\\nstatus: draft\\r\\nposted: false\\r\\nposted_at:\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# <Concept the student needs>\\r\\n\\r\\n<Open directly with the governing distinction or decision. One short orientation\\r\\nparagraph. No greeting, sign-off, praise, generic scene-setting, \\"Today...\\", or recap of\\r\\nwhich answers were correct.>\\r\\n\\r\\n## <A descriptive header that teaches the first part of the method>\\r\\n\\r\\n<Define the idea before applying it. Build a reusable reference with the combination of\\r\\nshort explanation, numbered steps, a compact table, or a spaced example that best fits\\r\\nthe material.>\\r\\n\\r\\n## <The next conceptual move>\\r\\n\\r\\n<Explain why it works, how to recognize when to use it, what does not follow, and how\\r\\nthe student can check the move. Add boundary cases or common traps when they mattered in\\r\\nthe session.>\\r\\n\\r\\n## <A repeatable process>\\r\\n\\r\\n1. <A decision the student can actually make.>\\r\\n2. <The next observable check.>\\r\\n3. <How to verify the inference or reject the trap.>\\r\\n\\r\\n## Before next session\\r\\n\\r\\n- [ ] <What was actually assigned, as the student would recognise it.>\\r\\n- [ ] <Only what the transcript supports. No invented drills.>\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## Notes for me (not posted)\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Weak spots:** <tags>\\r\\n- **Follow-ups on my side:** <things Joshua promised: send materials, assign a drill, schedule>\\r\\n- **Watch:** <a teaching judgment worth carrying into teaching-notes.md if it repeats>\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nEverything above the `---` rule is the student note and must stand alone when pasted.\\r\\nEverything below is admin-only.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe headings above are scaffolding, not a mandatory outline. Organize around the lesson\'s\\r\\nlogic. Use enough depth to teach the method fully, but remove any section that does not\\r\\nhelp the student use it.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Voice rules (from `wiki/teaching-voice.md`, Coaching register)\\r\\n\\r\\n- A post-session note is a set of lecture notes, not an email. Use a concept title,\\r\\n  descriptive headers, numbered procedures, and spaced examples. Do not use a greeting\\r\\n  or sign-off.\\r\\n- Open with Joshua\'s concrete explanation of the concept. Define the words the student\\r\\n  needs in plain language before diagrams or inference rules. Do not invent abstract\\r\\n  umbrella wording such as “how much of a group fits a description” when the direct\\r\\n  definition is “some means at least one; most means more than half; all means every one.”\\r\\n- Short sentences. One idea per line. Air between ideas.\\r\\n- Write for a student returning days later. Do not rely on \\"remember that question\\" or\\r\\n  unexplained references to a person, scenario, or answer choice.\\r\\n- Teach the reasoning; never just state the answer. \\"A reverses the timeline: the\\r\\n  symptom stops, then the boss assumes the cause was fixed\\" beats \\"A was wrong\\".\\r\\n- Praise only when it names a durable skill or meaningful change and ties to their\\r\\n  history. Never praise the mere fact that an answer was correct.\\r\\n- Honest about the test, never blunt about the student. When it slipped, say it is a\\r\\n  normal place to slip and move to the fix.\\r\\n- **No em dashes, ever.** Periods, colons, the middot (·).\\r\\n- No \\"unlock\\", \\"dive deep\\", \\"elevate\\", \\"game-changer\\", \\"seamless\\", \\"robust\\", no emoji.\\r\\n- No internal vocabulary: no \\"beat\\", no \\"door\\", no tool or model names, no \\"transcript\\"\\r\\n  or \\"Gemini\\" in the student note.\\r\\n- Only what the transcript supports. If he did not assign it, it is not in \\"Before\\r\\n  next session\\".\\r\\n- Read `wiki/COPY-CORRECTIONS.md` before writing; every past wording fix is there.\\r\\n- For conditional LSAT notes, distinguish an asserted fact from a general rule. A\\r\\n  rule states what follows if its trigger is present; it does not establish that the\\r\\n  trigger occurred. Some stimuli contain rules and no facts. Never invent a fact to\\r\\n  trigger a rule.\\r\\n\\r\\n## 4. Validate, log, and hand back\\r\\n\\r\\nBefore handoff, check that:\\r\\n\\r\\n- the opening begins with content rather than commentary about the session;\\r\\n- the note explains both the move and the reason it is valid;\\r\\n- examples make sense without the original question;\\r\\n- hierarchy is visible at a glance;\\r\\n- practice matches the transcript; and\\r\\n- the student-facing portion contains no private context, transcript references, or\\r\\n  administrative follow-ups.\\r\\n\\r\\n- Append the session line to the student\'s `transcripts.md` if one exists (primary,\\r\\n  append-only), and any promise he made to `open-loops.md`.\\r\\n- Append one line to `wiki/log.md`: `## YYYY-MM-DD recap | <students>` with paths.\\r\\n- Report: which recaps were written, which sessions had no transcript (list them, with\\r\\n  the reason if known), and anything that needs his call (a new name, a folder to\\r\\n  create). If Joshua explicitly requested a platform action, report its verification\\r\\n  separately from the draft.\\r\\n"}}'}]

## Tool: custom_tool_call_output

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 0.5 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"2406b2","wall_time_seconds":0.2747138,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":6370,"output":"---\\r\\ntitle: Teaching Voice\\r\\ntype: concept\\r\\ntags: [lsat-u, voice, pedagogy, content]\\r\\ncreated: 2026-06-10\\r\\nupdated: 2026-07-18\\r\\nstatus: active\\r\\nsubject: Teaching Voice\\r\\naliases: []\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Teaching Voice\\r\\n\\r\\nHow LSAT U sounds, across every surface. This is the canonical voice doc: route all student-facing and brand copy through it. Built from a grill with Joshua (2026-06-13), then tested and enriched against the full corpus of his real correspondence (944 messages he authored, mid-2025 to mid-2026, from the Gmail takeout; 2026-07-18). Claims below marked with a quote are evidenced by that corpus.\\r\\n\\r\\nIt replaces the old two-register / 15-named-tools \\"preserve verbatim\\" profile (deleted 2026-06-10) and folds in the brand/marketing register the earlier draft was missing.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Core voice (every register)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe constant under all three registers below. This is Joshua on the page.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Quiet authority.** State the value and let it land. Never oversell, never beg, never perform enthusiasm.\\r\\n- **Specific, never generic.** Real scores, the actual skill, the student\'s own history. Praise is a specific observation, not \\"great job.\\"\\r\\n- **Honest about the work, gentle about the person.** Be blunt that the LSAT is hard (\\"expect this to be exhausting and very challenging\\"). Never be blunt about a student\'s shortcomings. Honesty points at the material; warmth points at the person. When someone slips, nudge gently, never accuse.\\r\\n- **Light, grounded metaphor, understated in email.** In his real correspondence the recurring image is quiet: \\"partner with you on your LSAT journey,\\" \\"getting set up,\\" \\"foundational.\\" The vivid images (runway, climb, march toward November, an easy door to walk through) belong to authored teaching and brand copy, not to email. Keep metaphor light and grounded; never float off into abstraction.\\r\\n- **Balanced rhythm.** Short declaratives plus one slightly longer warm beat. Air between ideas. Each idea gets its own line. Real messages are short and single-purpose (median ~280 characters).\\r\\n- **Plain professional diction.** No corporate jargon, no startup hype (\\"unlock,\\" \\"crush,\\" \\"level up,\\" \\"game-changer\\" — \\"crush\\" appears once in 944 messages). Contractions are the norm, not the exception. Exclamation points are genuine, not performed: a warm message often carries one, occasionally more, especially in openers (\\"Sorry for such a long delay!\\"). He is not exclamation-averse.\\r\\n- **Forward-looking.** End on the next step or what\'s ahead.\\r\\n- **No em dashes, ever.** Use periods, colons before lists, the middot (·) as a separator, and numbered steps for procedures.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Openings, closings, and signature phrases\\r\\n\\r\\nThe mechanical fingerprint of his email, from the real corpus. Match these when drafting as Joshua.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Greeting.** \\"Hi [Name],\\" is the default (used ~519x). \\"Hey [Name],\\" for established/returning students (~229x, warmer). \\"Hello [Name],\\" (~105x) and \\"Dear [Name],\\" (~18x, formal) for first contact or a more formal note.\\r\\n- **Sign-off.** \\"Best,\\" and \\"Best regards,\\" are the workhorses (~360x / ~237x). \\"Thanks,\\" when it\'s a favor or logistics (~146x). \\"Warmly,\\" / \\"Warm regards,\\" (~54x) for a genuinely warm note. \\"Talk soon,\\" (~9x) for someone he\'ll see again soon.\\r\\n- **Signature.** Almost always signed **\\"Joshua\\"** (844 of 944 messages). The name is near-universal; include it.\\r\\n- **Signature phrases (his verbal fingerprint, use naturally, don\'t overuse):** \\"let me know\\" (by far the most common, ~390x), \\"looking forward,\\" \\"I hope\\" / \\"hope all is well\\" / \\"hope you,\\" \\"no worries at all,\\" \\"happy to\\" / \\"more than happy to,\\" \\"just wanted to make sure,\\" \\"make sure,\\" \\"no rush,\\" \\"of course.\\"\\r\\n- **Punctuation he actually uses:** semicolons (correctly, ~41x); ellipses essentially never. (For em-dashes, the hard rule in Core voice governs — never.)\\r\\n\\r\\n## The apology / accountability move\\r\\n\\r\\nOne of his most frequent and characteristic behaviors, and worth naming on its own. When he is late to reply, or missed or mishandled something, he opens by owning it plainly, often with a brief honest reason, then pivots straight to the fix. No over-apologizing, no excuses dressed up.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'m so sorry. I thought I had let you know ... I clearly didn\'t communicate that as well as I should have.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'ve been away from work for personal reasons, but I\'m back now and getting caught up.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe pattern: own it in the first line, give the real reason in one clause, move to what happens next. Warm, candid, brief.\\r\\n\\r\\n## When something on his side broke (approved shape, 2026-09-11)\\r\\n\\r\\nFrom the Sandra booking-error reply, edited by Joshua line by line over three drafts and then sent as-is. Use this shape whenever a student hit a bug or a mistake that was his. The sent text is the reference:\\r\\n\\r\\n> Hi Sandra,\\r\\n>\\r\\n> I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet. The page was showing a few times that the system then refused, and it looks like you landed on those. That is fixed now.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Your link is the same one as before:\\r\\n> [link]\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Pick any time it shows and it will book. If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Once again, my apologies.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Best,\\r\\n> Joshua\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Apology first, as the opening line.** \\"I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\" The ownership sits in the first two sentences, before any explanation.\\r\\n2. **State their position plainly, as a confirmation.** \\"To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet.\\" Answer the question they actually asked. Don\'t mention the package or credits unless the situation calls for it.\\r\\n3. **One-sentence explanation, then \\"That is fixed now.\\"** No mechanics, no system names.\\r\\n4. **Hand them the next step, plus the manual fallback.** The link, \\"pick any time it shows and it will book,\\" and the offer to do it by hand: \\"If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\"\\r\\n5. **Invite the next report:** \\"If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\"\\r\\n6. **Close with \\"Once again, my apologies.\\"** then \\"Best,\\" and \\"Joshua\\".\\r\\n\\r\\nCut from the draft, do not reuse:\\r\\n- \\"Sorry for the runaround\\" as a sign-off. The apology opens the email; it is not a closing quip.\\r\\n- \\"You will get a calendar invite with the Google Meet link right after.\\" Do not narrate what the system will send; it reads as a promise about machinery.\\r\\n- \\"You have all 10 sessions\\" / \\"nothing was used from your package.\\" Leave the package out unless it is needed; the reassurance they want is that nothing is booked, not an accounting.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Situational micro-templates\\r\\n\\r\\nVerbatim-grounded reference lines for the situations that recur most. Adapt, never paste blindly.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Student reschedules / cancels:** low-pressure, no guilt.\\r\\n  > No worries at all. It happens, so please don\'t worry about it. If you would like to reschedule, just let me know.\\r\\n- **He missed / no-showed (approved make-good template):** full ownership, real reason, offer to make it right (see the apology move above). When the cause was an unexpected health issue, the approved shape is: sincerely apologize, state that a serious health scare unexpectedly took him out of commission, offer a **completely free, full LSAT session**, and hand them the complimentary booking link `https://cal.com/joshua-jtx5ud/complimentary-session`. Emphasis stays limited: bold the complimentary offer, italicize the line that one focused session can put points on the board. Draft in Gmail; never send without Joshua\'s explicit go-ahead.\\r\\n- **Consultation reminder (day-of):**\\r\\n  > Just checking in before our consultation today. Looking forward to speaking with you. I just wanted to make sure everything is still good.\\r\\n- **Consultation follow-up:** warm, specific to their situation.\\r\\n  > Really nice meeting you. I enjoyed our conversation ... I\'m glad we got to talk through where you\'re at and what you\'re aiming for on test day.\\r\\n- **Inbound prospect (hasn\'t booked):** state availability plainly, no overselling, hand them the next step.\\r\\n  > Thanks for reaching out ... I\'d be happy to talk more about what you\'re working on and see if we\'d be a good fit. You can schedule a consultation here.\\r\\n- **Student under real-life stress:** meet the person first.\\r\\n  > Please don\'t apologize ... it sounds like you are dealing with an incredibly stressful and demanding situation.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The three registers\\r\\n\\r\\nWhich voice governs which surface.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. Coaching (earnest) -- inbox, recaps, in-drill feedback, email\\r\\n\\r\\nFully earnest. Warm, sincere, calm, patient. No jokes. The closest thing to being in the room with Joshua. Normalizes struggle, then moves to the work.\\r\\n\\r\\nReference line (target tone):\\r\\n\\r\\n> Totally normal to trip on this one. Let\'s slow down: what is the author actually concluding? Once you see it, the trap answers lose their grip. You\'ve got this.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Encouragement (student missed a hard one):** honest first, then forward. Name that it\'s genuinely hard, stay calm, move to the work. Not soft-reassuring, not cold.\\r\\n  > Missing this is expected. It\'s one of the hardest moves on the test. Let\'s slow down and see where it slipped.\\r\\n- **Accountability (student isn\'t doing the work):** gentle nudge, low pressure. Frame it as a slip, find a rhythm together. Never \\"the reps aren\'t happening,\\" never tough love.\\r\\n- **Praise (student nails it):** name the exact skill, tie it to their history, raise the bar.\\r\\n  > That\'s the cleanest you\'ve split premise from conclusion yet. Let\'s push it into the harder sets.\\r\\n- **Hard truth about the test:** state it plainly. \\"Do not expect for it to come easy. Expect to find this exhausting.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2. Teaching content (earnest substance, wit at the edges) -- bootcamp lessons, drill explanations\\r\\n\\r\\nThe substance stays earnest and clear (you are explaining a hard skill). The wit lives only at the edges: headers, openers, transitions. No jokes mid-explanation, nothing that costs comprehension.\\r\\n\\r\\n> Header: \\"The flaw hides in plain sight.\\"\\r\\n> Body: earnest, clear, step by step.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 3. Brand (sharp wit) -- landing, auth, marketing\\r\\n\\r\\nConfident and clever, the way a good lawyer is clever. Wit tied to the real skill, not wordplay for its own sake. Playful is allowed, but every clever line must be earned and true. Hollow cleverness fails (the killed \\"the next card is the page in front of you\\" was clever but empty).\\r\\n\\r\\n> Most prep teaches the test. We teach the tell.\\r\\n\\r\\nBrand copy speaks as the platform (\\"we\\", \\"you\\"), not as an individual (\\"I\\", \\"Joshua\\"). The product is the coach; no single person narrates the marketing.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Don\'t\\r\\n\\r\\n- No cold-testing or gotcha tone. (Ties to teach-first-calibrate-after.)\\r\\n- No condescension or empty cheerleading. Encouragement must sit on real substance.\\r\\n- No generic praise, no hollow cleverness, no hedging (\\"you might want to\\").\\r\\n- No hype/startup vocabulary.\\r\\n- No em dashes, ever.\\r\\n\\r\\nCorrections log: [[COPY-CORRECTIONS]] records every student-facing wording fix and\\r\\nthe reason it was wrong. Read it before writing or editing LSAT U copy.\\r\\n\\r\\nRelated: teach-first-calibrate-after, LSAT U. Source samples: `raw/templates/Golden Email Template Playbook.md`, `raw/templates/email_writing_examples_11_full.txt`, and the full authored-email corpus from the Gmail takeout (944 messages, analyzed 2026-07-18; takeout at `raw/sources/private/takeout/`, git-ignored).\\r\\n# Copy corrections\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery student-facing wording fix, with the reason it was wrong. Read this before\\r\\nwriting or editing copy for LSAT U so the same mistake is not made twice.\\r\\n\\r\\nCompanion to [[teaching-voice]], which says how the writing should sound. This\\r\\nsays what has actually gone wrong and why.\\r\\n\\r\\nStarted 2026-09-07 from a Read, Recall, Colour pass. Add to it every time a\\r\\ncorrection is made.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The rules these corrections came from\\r\\n\\r\\nThree rules already existed and all three leaked anyway, because each was\\r\\nenforced on the components that happened to exist when it was written. A surface\\r\\nadded later starts uncovered.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **No em dashes, ever.** [[teaching-voice]], Core voice.\\r\\n- **No internal vocabulary in student copy.** `projects/lsatu/src/features/activity-centre/CONTEXT.md`\\r\\n  carries the glossary and marks what to avoid.\\r\\n- **Every CSS token a stylesheet uses must be defined in it.** `projects/lsatu/CLAUDE.md`.\\r\\n\\r\\nGuards now live with the content rather than with each component:\\r\\n`content/instructions-voice.test.ts` checks the authored instructions, so every\\r\\nsurface that renders them is covered, including surfaces not written yet.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Corrections\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"Recall Rephrase Colour\\" → \\"Read, Recall, Colour\\"\\r\\nThe door\'s heading was hardcoded to a name the product does not have, one line\\r\\nunder a chip reading \\"Read, Recall, Colour\\". \\"Rephrase\\" belongs to a different\\r\\nActivity, Conditional Rephrase. A test asserted the wrong name, which is why\\r\\n2,600 passing tests never caught it.\\r\\n**Lesson:** when a test pins a string, check the string is right, not just that\\r\\nit matches.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"Intake only. Nothing comes back out yet…\\" → plain instruction\\r\\nClinical and abstract, and the sentence then told her to read \\"with full\\r\\nintonation\\" while step one is silent reading. The clause that made intonation\\r\\ninternal, \\"hear it naturally in your head\\", had been dropped in an earlier edit.\\r\\n**Lesson:** a word like \\"intake\\" reads as jargon. And when copy is trimmed,\\r\\ncheck what the trimmed clause was load-bearing for.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"Three beats through the stimulus\\" → \\"Three steps\\"\\r\\n\\"Beat\\" is the internal code name for one of the four method steps. The glossary\\r\\nsays students see **step**. The interface ten pixels below labelled the same four\\r\\nthings Step 1 to Step 4, so the page used two names for one thing.\\r\\n**Lesson:** never let an implementation name reach the page.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"22 pieces to read\\" → line removed\\r\\nA **piece** is one chunk, roughly a sentence, and the instructions on that same\\r\\npage use the word that way. The count was of stimuli, so \\"22 pieces\\" read as 22\\r\\nsentences.\\r\\n**Lesson:** a unit word must mean one thing per surface. Check what a word\\r\\nalready means on the page before reusing it.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"say it back\\" → \\"tell it back\\", \\"The Read\\" → \\"The Recall\\"\\r\\nThe library door still carried both retired names. \\"The Read\\" was step four\'s\\r\\nformer name and collided with step one, which is why it was renamed.\\r\\n**Lesson:** a rename is not finished until every row carries it. The door was\\r\\nstale for months because it is a different database row from the sections.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"then a fourth\\" → \\"then a fourth step\\"\\r\\nThe noun sat three words back and the reader had to carry it.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"once you have got all of it\\" → \\"once you have read all of it\\"\\r\\nAmbiguous between having read it and having remembered it, in the one clause\\r\\nthat triggers step four.\\r\\n**Lesson:** precision matters most where the sentence is an instruction.\\r\\n\\r\\n### The three-fact notice → one fact\\r\\n\\"Nothing is recording yet, the microphone opens on Start, and the section\\r\\nrecords in one take that you cannot pause.\\" Two of those are said again in step\\r\\nfour and in the long version, so she skipped the paragraph.\\r\\n**Lesson:** say it once, in the place it matters.\\r\\n\\r\\n### The method, told twice → the long version collapsed\\r\\nThe page rendered four numbered steps and then the whole written briefing saying\\r\\nthe same thing at length, both open. She read the method twice and could not\\r\\ntell which one to follow.\\r\\n**Lesson:** two explanations of one thing is worse than either alone.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"PT105.S1 · 24 stimuli · about 25 min\\" → removed\\r\\nThe section was already the second line of the title. The clock is at the foot\\r\\nand in the long version. The stimulus count measured the work in a unit she has\\r\\nno feel for.\\r\\n**Lesson:** delete a line that repeats what is above it. Do not reword it.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Booking emails: hand over the link, not the pass settings (2026-09-08)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Cut:** \\"70 minutes each, and no expiration date, so there\'s no rush to use them.\\"\\r\\n**Keep:** \\"You\'re set up on LSAT U with 10 sessions.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\nSession length and expiry are admin fields. The student sees them on the booking\\r\\npage when she picks a time, so putting them in the email is detail she did not ask\\r\\nfor and has to read past to reach the link. The credit count is worth saying because\\r\\nit tells her how much she has. Everything else about the pass stays in the backend.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Lesson:** in a booking email, say who it\'s for, how many sessions, and the link.\\r\\nStop there.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Drill hub: say what the button does, not what the feature is called (2026-09-09)\\r\\n\\r\\nSix changes on `/classroom/drill`, from the run-3 pass. The hub named its own\\r\\nfeatures, and it assumed the student had rejected something.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Was | Now |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| \\"Start Smart Drill\\" | \\"Practice your weakest types\\" |\\r\\n| \\"Start One Passage\\" | \\"Read one passage\\" |\\r\\n| \\"Start a Smart Drill instead\\" | \\"Or practice your weakest types\\" |\\r\\n| \\"Read one passage instead\\" | \\"Or read one passage now\\" |\\r\\n| \\"Open analytics\\" | \\"See where you lose points\\" |\\r\\n| \\"Open journal\\" | \\"Review your missed questions\\" |\\r\\n\\r\\n\\"Smart Drill\\" is the product\'s internal name for the adaptive set. On a button it\\r\\nasks the student to guess what she is about to get. The sentence above the button\\r\\nstill names it, which is where a product name belongs: after the thing has been\\r\\nexplained, not as the explanation.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\"Instead\\" was the worse one. It tells the student she has just declined the\\r\\nassigned work by reading past it. She has not. \\"Or\\" offers a second path without\\r\\nnarrating a decision she never made.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\"Open analytics\\" and \\"Open journal\\" name a screen. A student does not want\\r\\nanalytics, she wants to know where the points are going.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe fallback paragraph lost \\"an adaptive set that follows your weakest question\\r\\ntypes\\" for \\"the question types you miss most\\": the same fact, without the product\\r\\nvocabulary.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Lesson:** a button says what happens next, in the student\'s words. Feature names\\r\\nbelong in the sentence that explains them, never on the control.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Words never to use in student copy\\r\\n\\r\\nFrom the glossary. Internal names may stay in code, never on the page.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Never | Use instead |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| beat, beats | step |\\r\\n| chunk | piece |\\r\\n| intake | plain instruction |\\r\\n| briefing, phase, tab, card | the thing\'s own name |\\r\\n| say it back | tell it back |\\r\\n| The Read | The Recall |\\r\\n| Recall Rephrase Colour | Read, Recall, Colour |\\r\\n| em dash, en dash | a full stop, or a colon before a list |\\r\\n\\r\\n## Conditional Rephrase: name the student action, not the internal model (2026-09-15)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Cut:** “record the route,” “choose the route,” and a map presented as five rules.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Keep:** diagram the statement on paper, choose the matching diagram, and organize\\r\\nthe map into four groups. “Required means right” is a separate takeaway because it\\r\\nexplains placement; it is not a fifth group.\\r\\n\\r\\n“Route” described the system’s representation, not the student’s work. Calling five\\r\\nunlike ideas rules also flattened the teaching structure and made the layout harder to\\r\\nread.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Lesson:** name the action the student can see herself doing. Do not force a teaching\\r\\nreminder into the same hierarchy as the categories it explains.\\r\\n\\r\\nRelated: [[teaching-voice]] · [[ASSIGN-AN-ACTIVITY]] · [[STUDENT-PLATFORM-IDENTITY-MAP]]\\r\\n\\r\\n## Session recaps: write a reusable reference, not a play-by-play (2026-09-12)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Cut:** an opener saying the student got two questions right, followed by a summary of\\r\\nwhich answer they chose and how they explained it.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Keep:** the concept the student needs tomorrow, a visual model of the reasoning, a\\r\\nshort diagnostic check, and the exact practice they need to complete.\\r\\n\\r\\nA student will not remember an isolated answer-choice exchange a day later, and the\\r\\nexchange is not useful unless it demonstrates a reusable rule. A recap should read like\\r\\na compact study note, not a record of the conversation. Name a question only when the\\r\\ndetails make the concept easier to apply. Praise belongs only when it identifies a\\r\\ndurable skill or meaningful change, not merely that an answer was correct.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Lesson:** organize the recap around what the student can use next. Lead with the\\r\\nconcept, show the logic clearly, and finish with tangible practice.\\r\\n\\r\\n### A rule is not a fact (2026-09-12)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Cut:** describing a conditional Must Be True lesson as “applying a rule to a fact”\\r\\nwithout checking whether the stimulus supplied a fact at all.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Keep:** a fact is an asserted true case or condition. A rule is a general conditional\\r\\nrelationship. It tells you what follows if its trigger is present, but it does not say\\r\\nthat the trigger occurred. Some stimuli contain rules only, so the work is to chain\\r\\nthem. When a fact is present, apply a matching rule or a valid contrapositive.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Lesson:** label the role of each sentence before explaining the inference. Never\\r\\ninvent a fact to make a rule fire.\\r\\n\\r\\n### A post-session note is lecture material, not an email (2026-09-12)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Cut:** a greeting, a dated recap heading, references to a question the student is\\r\\nexpected to remember, and a sign-off.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Keep:** a concept title, a clear opening distinction, numbered procedures, spaced\\r\\nexamples, and practice that uses the lesson.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Lesson:** the note should remain useful when the session itself is no longer fresh.\\r\\nIt must teach from the page instead of relying on remembered context.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe concept should not arrive as an abrupt list. Begin with a short explanation of\\r\\nwhy the distinction matters, show the full method at a glance, and then teach each\\r\\npath in the same order. Use tables for comparisons and numbered headings for a\\r\\nprocedure so the student can see the structure before reading the detail.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Define the concept in Joshua\'s language (2026-09-28)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Cut:** “Some, most, and all tell you how much of a group fits a description.”\\r\\n\\r\\n**Keep:** “Some means at least one. Most means more than half. All means every one,”\\r\\ngrounded in a concrete set of ten cookies before drawing conclusions from the words.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe cut line is vague and does not sound like Joshua teaching. It makes the reader\\r\\ndecode “fits a description” before learning any of the three words. It also risks\\r\\nblurring the difference between a count that is possible and one that is guaranteed.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Lesson:** open with the actual distinction or definition Joshua taught. Use a\\r\\nconcrete example to show what each statement proves, then introduce notation and\\r\\nthe inferences. Do not write an abstract umbrella sentence merely to announce the\\r\\ntopic.\\r\\n# Post-session note quality reference\\r\\n\\r\\nCanonical source: `students/sofia/recaps/2026-09-11-recap.md`.\\r\\n\\r\\nUse that note as the quality bar for post-session notes. Preserve its method, not its\\r\\ntopic-specific wording. A strong note:\\r\\n\\r\\n- reads as lecture notes, not an email or a transcript summary;\\r\\n- opens directly with the governing concept;\\r\\n- separates ideas with descriptive headings and generous spacing;\\r\\n- defines the important distinction before asking the student to use it;\\r\\n- turns Joshua\'s explanation into a reusable method;\\r\\n- uses compact tables, numbered steps, and diagrams only when they reduce cognitive load;\\r\\n- includes valid moves, invalid moves, boundary cases, and a way to test the answer;\\r\\n- gives examples that stand alone without requiring memory of a question from days ago;\\r\\n- ends with concrete practice supported by the session; and\\r\\n- keeps private teaching judgments below the `Notes for me (not posted)` divider.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Reference structure\\r\\n\\r\\nThe Sofia note uses this content-shaped progression:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Concept title.** `Conditional Must Be True: Facts, Rules, and Bridges`\\r\\n2. **Direct orientation.** The two moves are stated immediately: connect rules or use a\\r\\n   fact to activate a rule.\\r\\n3. **Method at a glance.** A small table distinguishes chaining from triggering.\\r\\n4. **Foundational distinction.** Facts and rules are defined before either is applied.\\r\\n5. **First method.** Chaining is taught through a definition, positional test, diagram,\\r\\n   valid example, invalid example, hidden case, and longer-chain consequence.\\r\\n6. **Second method.** Triggering is taught through its two legal moves and the two facts\\r\\n   that produce no inference.\\r\\n7. **Decision aid.** A four-row table makes valid and invalid directions visible.\\r\\n8. **Execution advice.** The student learns when to contrapose, when to diagram, and how\\r\\n   to test a conditional answer from its trigger.\\r\\n9. **Repeatable process.** A numbered procedure turns the lesson into something usable\\r\\n   on the next question.\\r\\n10. **Practice.** Checkboxes state the work actually assigned.\\r\\n11. **Private continuation.** Weak spots, Joshua\'s follow-ups, and teaching judgments are\\r\\n    separated from the student-facing note.\\r\\n\\r\\n## What to copy and what to vary\\r\\n\\r\\nCopy the depth, hierarchy, and independence from remembered question context. Vary the\\r\\nsections to fit the lesson. Do not force every recap into the same headings. A causation\\r\\nsession, an RC mapping session, and a conditional-logic session should not look identical.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe note is complete when the student can return several days later and use it to solve\\r\\nthe same kind of problem without reconstructing the original session.\\r\\n"}'}]

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 0.7 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Warning: truncated output (original token count: 17759)\nTotal output lines: 1\n\n{"chunk_id":"00fffc","wall_time_seconds":0.4689371,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":24353,"output":"Warning: truncated output (original token count: 24353)\\nTotal output lines: 1096\\n\\n# Some, Most, and All\\r\\n\\r\\nQuantity statements tell us whether a claim applies to some members of a group, most of them, or all of them. Suppose a class has been assigned a case to read. “Some students read it,” “most students read it,” and “all students read it” are three different claims about that same class. We do not need an exact headcount to understand the difference.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor each sentence, ask: **What must be true? What could still be true?** The answer changes with the word we use.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Some guarantees at least one\\r\\n\\r\\nImagine a shelf with eight books. I tell you that **some of the books are hardcover**. How many hardcover books must there be?\\r\\n\\r\\nAt least **one**. There could be one, four, or all eight. “Some” rules out zero. It does not rule out “most” or “all.”\\r\\n\\r\\n![Eight books showing that one hardcover book and eight hardcover books both satisfy some.](./assets/some-books.svg)\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is easy to miss because in ordinary conversation “some” often suggests “some, but not all.” On the LSAT, that extra phrase is not part of the statement. If all eight books are hardcover, it is still true that some are hardcover.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Try it:** “Some applicants received an interview.” Could every applicant have received one? Does the sentence tell us that anyone was denied an interview?\\r\\n\\r\\n<details><summary>Check your answer</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery applicant could have received an interview. The sentence does not tell us that anyone was denied one. “Some” guarantees at least one applicant received an interview, but it leaves open how many others did.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\nWhenever you read **some**, replace it with **at least one** in your head. That tells you exactly what the sentence guarantees:\\r\\n\\r\\n> **Some of the books are hardcover.**\\r\\n>\\r\\n> **At least one of the books is hardcover.**\\r\\n\\r\\nNow focus on that one book. It belongs to both groups: it is a book, and it is hardcover. If we describe the same object from the hardcover side, we can say:\\r\\n\\r\\n> **Some hardcover items are books.**\\r\\n>\\r\\n> **At least one hardcover item is a book.**\\r\\n\\r\\nWe have not found a new object. We have described the same overlap in the other direction. That is why a **some** statement works both ways:\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\nBooks  ←some→  Hardcover\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThe double arrow tells us that at least one thing belongs to both groups. It does not tell us that every book is hardcover or that every hardcover item is a book.\\r\\n\\r\\n### What would make “some” false?\\r\\n\\r\\nIf **some books are hardcover** is false, then **no books are hardcover**. There is not even one book in both groups. Notice the difference between **no books are hardcover** and **some books are not hardcover**. The second sentence still allows other books to be hardcover, so it does not negate “some.”\\r\\n\\r\\n## Most guarantees more than half\\r\\n\\r\\nNow I tell you that **most of the eight books are hardcover**. We need at least **five** hardcover books. Four would be exactly half, and half is not most. Five, six, seven, or eight could satisfy the sentence.\\r\\n\\r\\n![Eight books showing that five hardcover books and eight hardcover books both satisfy most.](./assets/most-books.svg)\\r\\n\\r\\nNotice that all eight could still be hardcover. “Most” does not tell us that an exception exists.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Try it:** If most of the eight books are hardcover, must some of them be hardcover? Must any be paperback?\\r\\n\\r\\n<details><summary>Check your answer</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\nAt least five are hardcover, so **some are hardcover**. No paperback book is required. All eight could be hardcover.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\nHere is where the direction of the statement matters. From “most books are hardcover,” we know that **some hardcover things are books**. We cannot say that **most hardcover things are books**. Five of our eight shelf books could be hardcover, while a library holds hundreds of other hardcover items. The first statement counts the eight books; the reversed statement counts a different group.\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\nBooks  ─most→  Hardcover\\r\\nHardcover  ←some→  Books\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThe first arrow gives the majority claim. The second line is the overlap that the majority guarantees. When we read a most statement backward, the word becomes **some**.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Quick check:** A program has 100 applicants. Most speak Spanish. What is the smallest possible number who speak Spanish? What is the largest?\\r\\n\\r\\n<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\n**51 to 100.** Fifty is only half. “Most” also permits all 100, so it does not establish an exception.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\n### What would make “most” false?\\r\\n\\r\\n“Most of the eight books are hardcover” needs at least five hardcover books. Its negation permits **four or fewer**. Four is exactly half, so it already makes “most” false. The opposite of “most are hardcover” is **half or fewer are hardcover**, not “most are paperback.” Both kinds could make up exactly half.\\r\\n\\r\\n## All leaves no exception\\r\\n\\r\\nIf **all eight books are hardcover**, every book on the shelf is hardcover. One paperback on that shelf would make the statement false.\\r\\n\\r\\n![Eight books showing that all eight must be hardcover to satisfy all.](./assets/all-books.svg)\\r\\n\\r\\nAn all statement gives us a rule: **if it is one of these eight books, then it is hardcover**.\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\nOne of these books  →  Hardcover\\r\\nNot hardcover       →  Not one of these books\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThe second line is the contrapositive. Both lines go with the same rule. We cannot turn the first line around and conclude that every hardcover thing is a book on this shelf.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Try it:** You pick up a paperback. What does the rule tell you? What if you pick up a hardcover book from another shelf?\\r\\n\\r\\n<details><summary>Check your answer</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\nThe paperback cannot be one of these eight books. A hardcover book from another shelf does not become one of these eight just because it is hardcover. Being hardcover is required, but it is not enough to identify one of these books.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\nThere is a small qualification. “All A are B” gives a rule about A. By itself, it does not tell us that any A exist. When we already know the group exists, all also guarantees most and some.\\r\\n\\r\\n### What would make “all” false?\\r\\n\\r\\nOne exception is enough. “Not all eight books are hardcover” means **at least one of the eight is not hardcover**. The other seven could still be hardcover. This is the negation of the all claim. By contrast, “not hardcover → not one of these eight books” is its **contrapositive**: another way to state the original rule, not a way to deny it.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Put the three statements side by side\\r\\n\\r\\nThe same shelf can help us see the whole range.\\r\\n\\r\\n![For eight existing books: some permits one through eight hardcover, most permits five through eight, and all requires eight.](./assets/book-quantity-ranges.svg)\\r\\n\\r\\nRead the implications in one direction:\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\nALL  →  MOST  →  SOME       (when the group exists)\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nIf all eight books are hardcover, then most are, and some are. If only “some” is given, all eight **could** be hardcover, but we cannot conclude that they **are**. Keep the distinction between a possible situation and a required one.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Carry a claim through an all rule\\r\\n\\r\\nNow we can combine statements. Suppose **some library books are mysteries** and **all mysteries are fiction**. We have at least one book that is a mystery. The all rule applies to every mystery, including that one. So **some library books are fiction**.\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\nLibrary books  ←some→  Mysteries  →  Fiction\\r\\nLibrary books  ←some→  Fiction\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThe all arrow points **away from** the mystery group we reached. That is why the chain works. If the second sentence said only “most mysteries are fiction,” the mystery books we found could be among the exceptions.\\r\\n\\r\\n![A marked library book is inside the mysteries group, which is entirely inside the fiction group.](./assets/some-all-witness.svg)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Quick check:** Some archive documents are letters. All letters are handwritten. What follows?\\r\\n\\r\\n<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\n**Some archive documents are handwritten.** Take a document guaranteed to be a letter. The all rule applies to that document.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\nThe same reasoning preserves the first quantity word:\\r\\n\\r\\n| First statement | Rule | What follows |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| Some library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | Some library books are fiction. |\\r\\n| Most library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | Most library books are fiction. |\\r\\n| All library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | All library books are fiction. |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Try it:** “Most library books are mysteries. All fiction is mystery.” Can we conclude that most library books are fiction?\\r\\n\\r\\n<details><summary>Check your answer</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\nNo. The all arrow goes from fiction to mystery. We cannot start at mystery and travel backward to fiction.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\n## Two majorities of the same group must meet\\r\\n\\r\\nSuppose a club has ten members. **Most members study law**, and **most members work part time**. Each “most” needs at least six of the ten members. Those two sets cannot fit inside the club without sharing at least two people.\\r\\n\\r\\n![Ten club members. Six study law, six work part time, and at least two do both.](./assets/club-majority-overlap.svg)\\r\\n\\r\\n**What is given?** More than half of the *same ten members* study law. More than half of those same ten work part time. The claims count club members, not all law students or all part-time workers everywhere.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Why must they meet?** Each group needs at least six members. If the groups were separate, we would need twelve different club members. There are only ten. At least two members must be in both groups.\\r\\n\\r\\n**What follows?** **Some law students work part time.** We can reverse that some claim: **some part-time workers study law**. Both sentences describe the same overlapping members. We know at least one exists; we do not know that most law students or most part-time workers have the other trait.\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\nGiven:       Most club members study law.\\r\\n             Most club members work part time.\\r\\nMust follow: Some law students work part time.\\r\\nWhy:         Both majorities count the same club members.\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**Quick check:** A club has 25 members. Most are lawyers, and most play an instrument. What is the smallest possible number who are both lawyers and play an instrument?\\r\\n\\r\\n<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\n**One.** Each majority needs at least 13 members. If none overlapped, those groups would require 26 different people, but the club has only 25. All 25 could also have both traits.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\n**Try it:** If most club members study law and most club members work part time, could the two groups of members be completely separate?\\r\\n\\r\\n<details><summary>Check your answer</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\nNo. Two separate majorities would require more members than the club has. At least one member must have both traits.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\n### When all describes that same group\\r\\n\\r\\nThere is another way to guarantee an overlap. Suppose **most club members study law**, and **all club members work part time**. We already know there are law students in the club. The all rule tells us that *each one of those members* also works part time. So **some law students work part time**.\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\nGiven:       Most club members study law.\\r\\n             All club members work part time.\\r\\nMust follow: Some law students work part time.\\r\\nWhy:         The law students already found are club members,\\r\\n             so the all rule applies to each of them.\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nWe can make the same move with **some**. If **some club members study law** and **all club members work part time**, take the member guaranteed by “some.” That person has both traits. Again, **some law students work part time**. The sentences can be stated in the other order: **all club members work part time; some club members study law**. The same person still proves the overlap.\\r\\n\\r\\n![An all rule covers every club member. A highlighted law student is therefore also a part-time worker.](./assets/all-and-overlap.svg)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Try it:** All A are B. All A are C. Must some B be C?\\r\\n\\r\\n<details><summary>Check your answer</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\nNot yet. The two all rules tell us what is true **if** something is A, but neither tells us that any A exists. Add “at least one A exists,” and the overlap follows.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\n## Two majorities can also compare group sizes\\r\\n\\r\\nHere is a different comparison. **Most debate team members are seniors**, but **most seniors are not on the debate team**. The seniors on the team are more than half of the team and less than half of the seniors. The same overlap takes up a larger share of the team than of the senior class. Therefore, **there are more seniors than debate team members**.\\r\\n\\r\\n![An example in which six of ten debate team members are seniors, while six of twenty seniors are on the team.](./assets/group-size-comparison.svg)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe numbers in the picture are one possible case. The conclusion follows from the two majority claims, not from those particular numbers.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Similar chains can leave a gap\\r\\n\\r\\nTwo some statements need not describe the same person or thing:\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\nSome volunteers speak Spanish.\\r\\nSome Spanish speakers are trained.\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThe trained Spanish speakers could all be people who do not volunteer. We cannot conclude that any volunteers are trained.\\r\\n\\r\\n![Two different Spanish speakers satisfy the two some claims without any volunteer being trained.](./assets/some-some-gap.svg)\\r\\n\\r\\nReplacing the second “some” with “most” does not fix the gap. The Spanish-speaking volunteers could sit in the untrained minority. Even two most statements that count different groups do not automatically produce a new majority claim.\\r\\n\\r\\nBefore drawing a conclusion, ask: **Am I carrying a known group through an all rule? Or do two majorities count the same group?** If neither is true, check whether the groups could miss each other.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Quick check:** A club has 13 members. Most are women, and some are dancers. How many female dancers are guaranteed? How many are possible?\\r\\n\\r\\n<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\n**Zero are guaranteed; as many as 13 are possible.** Seven women and one dancer meet the statements even if that dancer is one of the six men. Both traits could also belong to every member. A most claim and a some claim about the same group do not force the two traits to meet.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\n## The moves to keep\\r\\n\\r\\n| What you have | What you may conclude |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| Some A are B | Some B are A |\\r\\n| Most A are B | Some A are B, and some B are A |\\r\\n| All A are B | A → B, and not B → not A |\\r\\n| Some/most/all A are B; all B are C | The same first quantity of A are C |\\r\\n| Most A are B; most A are C | Some B are C |\\r\\n| Most A are B; all A are C | Some B are C |\\r\\n| Some A are B; all A are C | Some B are C |\\r\\n\\r\\nTwo **all** claims about A guarantee that every A has both traits. They guarantee **some B are C** only when we also know that at least one A exists.\\r\\n\\r\\nUse the sentence behind each arrow to check what it guarantees.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Nearby words need a closer look\\r\\n\\r\\nThe words around a quantity statement can look familiar without making the same promise. Sort them by **what they guarantee**, then check the sentence in front of you:\\r\\n\\r\\n| Word or phrase | What it guarantees |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| **Some**, **at least one**, **one or more** | One or more members fit. All may fit too. |\\r\\n| **A few**, **several**, **many** | A positive number in ordinary use, but no universal cutoff. They imply at least one. |\\r\\n| **Most**, **more than half**, **a majority of** | Strictly more than half of the named group fit. |\\r\\n| **All**, **every**, **each**, **without exception** | Every member of the named group fits. The group may still need a separate existence premise. |\\r\\n| **Few**, **not many**, **not often** | A small number or low frequency in context. No exact numerical boundary follows. |\\r\\n| **No**, **none**, **zero** | Not a single member fits. |\\r\\n| **Not all** | At least one member does **not** fit. |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Few** is worth separating from **a few**. “A few books are hardcover” affirms that at least some are. “Few books are hardcover” stresses how small the number is. It often suggests some in ordinary speech, but it does not set a dependable numerical minimum. “Not many” can include zero. A hundred menu items could make five feel like few; in a menu of six, five would not feel like few. Do not quietly replace any of these phrases with a fixed number.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Most** is different: it crosses a precise line, **more than half**. Words such as **the majority** plainly express that idea. Words such as **usually**, **typically**, **generally**, **commonly**, **frequently**, **often**, **likely**, and **probably** can suggest prevalence in context, but pay attention to what the sentence actually counts. “Probably” about one event, for example, is a likelihood claim, not a headcount of a group.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Not all** *does* give us a precise minimum: at least one exception. “Not all club members are lawyers” means **at least one club member is not a lawyer**. It does not tell us whether the other members are lawyers.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Quick check:** A menu lists 100 beers. “Many are Belgian,” “few are Belgian,” and “not many are Belgian” are three claims. Can you assign each one an exact minimum and maximum? What does “not all are Belgian” guarantee?\\r\\n\\r\\n<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\nThe first three do **not** have fixed numerical boundaries. “Many” suggests more than an isolated example, while “few” and “not many” suggest a small number relative to the context. None alone licenses a specific cutoff such as five or ten. “Not all” is exact about one thing: **at least one beer is not Belgian**.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\n### Pop quiz: decide whether the overlap follows\\r\\n\\r\\nFor each pair, decide whether it guarantees **some A are C**. Draw a witness or explain where the groups could miss each other before opening the answers.\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Some A are B. All B are C.\\r\\n2. Some A are B. Most A are C.\\r\\n3. All A are B. Some B are C.\\r\\n4. Some A are B. Most B are C.\\r\\n5. Some A are B. Some B are C.\\r\\n6. Most A are B. Most A are C.\\r\\n7. All A are B. All A are C.\\r\\n\\r\\n<details><summary>Show the worked answers</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Yes.** The A that is B must also be C because every B is C.\\r\\n2. **No.** The A that is B could be outside the majority of A that is C.\\r\\n3. **No.** The B that is C could be outside A. The all rule runs from A to B, not back from B to A.\\r\\n4. **No.** The known A that is B could be among the B that are not C.\\r\\n5. **No.** The B in the first statement could differ from the B in the second.\\r\\n6. **Yes.** Two majorities of the same A group must share at least one member, who is both B and C.\\r\\n7. **Not from these statements alone.** Every A would be both B and C, but the statements do not establish that an A exists. If at least one A exists, the answer becomes yes.\\r\\n\\r\\n“No” here means **no guaranteed A–C overlap**.…7759 tokens truncated…on matches\':\'Your conclusion needs another look\';document.getElementById(\'quantity-quiz-verdict\').textContent=q.answer===\'yes\'?\'Yes. The overlap follows.\':\'No. The overlap is not guaranteed.\';document.getElementById(\'quantity-quiz-explanation\').textContent=q.explanation;document.getElementById(\'quantity-quiz-next\').innerHTML=quizIndex===quizQuestions.length-1?\'See your review <span aria-hidden=\\"true\\">→</span>\':\'Next question <span aria-hidden=\\"true\\">→</span>\';quizBridge.classList.add(q.answer===\'yes\'?\'is-yes\':\'is-no\');quizForm.hidden=true;quizFeedback.hidden=false;quizFeedback.focus();});\\r\\ndocument.getElementById(\'quantity-quiz-next\').addEventListener(\'click\',()=>{if(quizIndex===quizQuestions.length-1){quizStage.hidden=true;quizDone.hidden=false;document.getElementById(\'quantity-quiz-score\').textContent=quizMatches+\' of 7 conclusions matched\';document.getElementById(\'quantity-quiz-progress\').textContent=\'07 / 07\';}else{quizIndex++;renderQuiz();quizInput.focus()}});\\r\\ndocument.getElementById(\'quantity-quiz-restart\').addEventListener(\'click\',()=>{quizIndex=0;quizMatches=0;quizDone.hidden=true;quizStage.hidden=false;renderQuiz();quizInput.focus()});\\r\\n</script>\\r\\n</body></html>`;\\r\\n\\r\\nconst out = path.join(here, \\"08-quantity-statements-visual-preview.html\\");\\r\\nfs.writeFileSync(out, page, \\"utf8\\");\\r\\nconsole.log(out);\\r\\n# Choose the move the information supports\\r\\n\\r\\nA rule tells you what follows if a condition is met. A fact tells you what is true in a particular case. Before drawing an inference, decide which kind of information you have and where it lets you start.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Apply a fact to a rule\\r\\n\\r\\nSuppose every application submitted after the deadline requires special approval. Maya submitted her application after the deadline. Maya\'s application therefore requires special approval.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe first sentence supplies the rule. The second supplies its starting condition for one application. Together they support a conclusion about that application.\\r\\n\\r\\nLate application → requires special approval.\\r\\n\\r\\nMaya\'s application is late → Maya\'s application requires special approval.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe fact must match the complete condition. If the rule concerns applications submitted after the deadline, knowing that an application was started after the deadline would not be enough. Started and submitted are different claims.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is the same issue as keeping should in the mediation statement. Actually attending mediation does not establish that someone should attend. A fact cannot activate a rule by matching only part of its wording.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Check your reasoning\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery application submitted after the deadline requires special approval. Omar\'s application requires special approval. Must Omar have submitted it after the deadline?\\r\\n\\r\\n**Worked answer:** No. Special approval is the result, not the starting condition. Other applications might also require it. An on-time application that needs approval for another reason fits the rule and defeats the proposed inference.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Find the two starting points a rule gives you\\r\\n\\r\\nUse the same rule: late application → requires special approval.\\r\\n\\r\\nThere are two facts that let you draw a definite conclusion:\\r\\n\\r\\n- The application is late. It requires special approval.\\r\\n- The application does not require special approval. It is not late.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe second move uses the contrapositive. A late application without the required approval condition would violate the rule, so an application lacking that condition cannot be late.\\r\\n\\r\\nTwo other facts leave the opposite side open:\\r\\n\\r\\n- It requires special approval. It may or may not be late.\\r\\n- It is not late. It may or may not require special approval.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Rule | Fact supplied | What follows |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| A → B | A | B |\\r\\n| A → B | not B | not A |\\r\\n| A → B | B | A remains open |\\r\\n| A → B | not A | B remains open |\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not choose a direction merely because a sentence mentions a familiar term. Locate the fact on the rule first. A fact about the trigger or the absence of the requirement allows a move. A fact about the requirement or the absence of the trigger does not.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Check your reasoning\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery application submitted after the deadline requires special approval. Tess\'s application does not require special approval. What follows? What would follow if her application were simply not late?\\r\\n\\r\\n**Worked answer:** Tess\'s application is not late, by contraposition. If all we knew was that it was not late, the rule would not determine whether it required special approval. An on-time application could require approval for a different reason.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Link rules before applying a fact\\r\\n\\r\\nSuppose every application submitted after the deadline requires special approval. Every application requiring special approval needs a supervisor\'s signature.\\r\\n\\r\\nLate → requires special approval → needs a supervisor\'s signature.\\r\\n\\r\\nTherefore, every late application needs a supervisor\'s signature. The result of the first rule supplies the starting condition of the second. That is why the chain works.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is still a rule. It does not establish that any application was late. If you add the fact that Maya\'s application was late, you can apply the whole chain and conclude that her application requires approval and needs a signature.\\r\\n\\r\\nMatch the complete middle idea, including its subject and wording. Requires approval is not the same as has received approval. A rule about applications requiring approval cannot automatically connect to a rule about people granting approval.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Check your reasoning\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery urgent request needs a review. Every request needing a review requires a supervisor\'s signature. Does every urgent request require a supervisor\'s signature? Do these rules establish that an urgent request exists?\\r\\n\\r\\n**Worked answer:** Every urgent request requires a signature: urgent → needs review → requires signature. The rules do not establish that any urgent request exists. An additional fact would be needed to apply the rule to a particular request.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Shared words do not always create a chain\\r\\n\\r\\nConsider two different rules:\\r\\n\\r\\nLate → requires special approval.\\r\\n\\r\\nLate → needs a supervisor\'s signature.\\r\\n\\r\\nBoth start from late. Neither tells you that requiring approval is enough to need a signature. You cannot connect their results into requires approval → needs a signature.\\r\\n\\r\\nTry a counterexample: an on-time application requires special approval but does not need a supervisor\'s signature. Both rules still hold because their starting condition is absent. This defeats the proposed connection between the results.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe same problem appears when two rules share a result: A → C and B → C do not establish A → B. Different starting conditions can lead to the same result.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Check your reasoning\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery registered participant receives an email. Every registered participant has a name badge. Must everyone who receives an email have a name badge?\\r\\n\\r\\n**Worked answer:** No. Someone who is not registered could receive an email without having a badge. Both rules concern registered participants; they do not connect email recipients to badge holders. For a registered participant, however, both results follow.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Negate the whole condition\\r\\n\\r\\nSuppose an archive file may be released only if it has been reviewed AND has consent.\\r\\n\\r\\nMay be released → reviewed AND consent.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe file lacks a necessary requirement if either review or consent is missing. The contrapositive is:\\r\\n\\r\\nnot reviewed OR not consent → may not be released.\\r\\n\\r\\nYou do not need both requirements to be missing. One is enough to rule out permission. A reviewed file without consent satisfies the OR starting point and cannot be released under this rule.\\r\\n\\r\\nBy contrast, if a rule requires at least one of two alternatives, both alternatives must be absent to show the requirement is unmet:\\r\\n\\r\\nMay enter → badge OR invitation.\\r\\n\\r\\nnot badge AND not invitation → may not enter.\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep permission distinct from actual behavior. May not enter does not prove that a person never enters.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Check your reasoning\\r\\n\\r\\nA document may be shared only if it is reviewed AND authorized. It is reviewed but not authorized. May it be shared under this rule?\\r\\n\\r\\n**Worked answer:** No. Authorization is one of the two required conditions. Its absence triggers the contrapositive. The document does not need to be both unreviewed and unauthorized for permission to fail.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Choose your next move\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Separate the facts from the rules.\\r\\n2. Translate each rule while keeping the complete subject, negation, and words such as should or may.\\r\\n3. If you have a fact, locate it on a rule. Move forward from the trigger, or use contraposition from the absence of the requirement.\\r\\n4. If you have rules to connect, match the result of one to the trigger of another. Contrapose first if that creates a valid match.\\r\\n5. State exactly what follows. Preserve the strength and scope of the evidence.\\r\\n6. Test a tempting stronger conclusion: can the premises be true while that conclusion is false?\\r\\n\\r\\n### Put the moves together\\r\\n\\r\\nAll priority applications require review. Every application requiring review needs supervisor approval. Ari\'s application is a priority application. What follows?\\r\\n\\r\\n**Worked answer:** Ari\'s application requires review and needs supervisor approval. The fact activates priority → requires review → needs approval. This does not establish that either review or approval has actually happened.\\r\\n\\r\\nAll priority applications require review. Bea\'s application does not require review. What follows?\\r\\n\\r\\n**Worked answer:** Bea\'s application is not a priority application. Contrapose priority → requires review. This does not show that Bea never receives a review voluntarily.\\r\\n\\r\\nTransfer question: Every application needing supervisor approval requires a signature. Every application requiring a signature must be archived. Dev\'s application does not have to be archived. This tells you what is required for mediation to be appropriate. It does not tell you who actually attends, or whether willingness alone is enough. Keeping those distinctions intact is the work of conditional reasoning.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Combine what the statements guarantee\\r\\n\\r\\nA Must Be True answer must follow from the information you were given. Sometimes you combine facts. Sometimes you connect rules. Identify what each sentence gives you before choosing a method.\\r\\n\\r\\nSuppose one type of flavonoid found in apples is an antioxidant, and antioxidants help prevent heart disease. You can conclude that at least one type of flavonoid found in apples helps prevent heart disease.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhy at least one? The first statement identifies one type with the relevant property. The second tells you what that property does. Together they support a claim about that type. They do not show that every flavonoid has the property, or that eating any apple prevents heart disease.\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep the strength of the conclusion equal to the strength of the evidence. Helps prevent does not mean always prevents.\\r\\n\\r\\nA rule works differently. If a person should undergo mediation, that person is willing to compromise tells you a relationship. It does not tell you that anyone actually should undergo mediation. A rule does not establish its own starting condition.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Check your reasoning\\r\\n\\r\\nAn apple flavonoid is an antioxidant, and antioxidants help prevent heart disease. Can you conclude that every apple flavonoid prevents heart disease? Explain.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Worked answer:** No. The evidence establishes the relevant property for at least one type, not every type. It says helps prevent, not always prevents. A second type without that property would fit the evidence and defeat the stronger answer.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Put the requirement on the right\\r\\n\\r\\nConsider this hypothetical rule: Only people willing to compromise should undergo mediation to resolve their conflict.\\r\\n\\r\\nMediation means trying to resolve a dispute with help from a neutral person. The rule limits who should use it. Willingness to compromise is required.\\r\\n\\r\\nFirst flatten the sentence into complete English:\\r\\n\\r\\nIf a person should undergo mediation, then that person is willing to compromise.\\r\\n\\r\\nNow abbreviate the complete ideas:\\r\\n\\r\\nM = the person should undergo mediation.\\r\\n\\r\\nW = the person is willing to compromise.\\r\\n\\r\\nM → W\\r\\n\\r\\nThe left side is sufficient: knowing M lets you conclude W. The right side is necessary: M cannot be true without W. Necessary does not mean enough by itself. A person can meet a requirement without qualifying for the activity.\\r\\n\\r\\nOnly if works the same way. Litigation should be pursued only if a person is sure their position is correct becomes: If the person should pursue litigation, then the person is sure their position is correct.\\r\\n\\r\\nL = the person should pursue litigation. C = the person is sure their position is correct.\\r\\n\\r\\nL → C\\r\\n\\r\\nBeing sure is required. It does not establish that the person should litigate. Also, being sure that a position is correct is not the same as the position actually being correct.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Check your reasoning\\r\\n\\r\\nOnly trained volunteers should lead the workshop. Write the complete if-then rule. Does training alone prove that a volunteer should lead?\\r\\n4. Some A are B. Most B are C.\\r\\n5. Some A are B. Some B are C.\\r\\n6. Most A are B. Most A are C.\\r\\n7. All A are B. All A are C.\\r\\n\\r\\n<details><summary>Show the worked answers</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Yes.** The A that is B must also be C because every B is C.\\r\\n2. **No.** The A that is B could be outside the majority of A that is C.\\r\\n3. **No.** The B that is C could be outside A. The all rule runs from A to B, not back from B to A.\\r\\n4. **No.** The known A that is B could be among the B that are not C.\\r\\n5. **No.** The B in the first statement could differ from the B in the second.\\r\\n6. **Yes.** Two majorities of the same A group must share at least one member, who is both B and C.\\r\\n7. **Not from these statements alone.** Every A would be both B and C, but the statements do not establish that an A exists. If at least one A exists, the answer becomes yes.\\r\\n\\r\\n“No” here means **no guaranteed A–C overlap**. The premises may still imply a different, smaller fact. For example, statement 3\'s “some B are C” is already given.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\n## Short drill: diagram, combine, decide\\r\\n\\r\\nHere are five statements about one volunteer program. **Volunteer**, **Spanish speaker**, **trained person**, **weekend worker**, and **student** name groups of people. Most volunteers are students.\\r\\n5. Most weekend workers are trained.\\r\\n\\r\\nFirst, diagram each statement. Then answer these without looking below:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Which two statements prove that **some volunteers are trained**?\\r\\n2. Which two statements prove that **some students work weekends**?\\r\\n3. Do statements 3 and 5 prove that **most volunteers are trained**? Explain the gap or draw a counterexample.\\r\\n4. Can you write either valid **some** conclusion in the reverse order?\\r\\n\\r\\n<details><summary>Show the diagrams and worked answers</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\n1. Volunteers       ←some→  Spanish speakers\\r\\n2. Spanish speakers →       Trained people\\r\\n3. Volunteers       ─most→  Weekend workers\\r\\n4. Volunteers       ─most→  Students\\r\\n5. Weekend workers  ─most→  Trained people\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**1. Statements 1 and 2.** At least one volunteer speaks Spanish. Every Spanish speaker is trained. That volunteer is trained, so **some volunteers are trained**.\\r\\n\\r\\n**2. Statements 3 and 4.** Both majorities count the volunteers. The weekend workers and students must share at least one volunteer. So **some students work weekends**.\\r\\n\\r\\n**3. No.** Statement 3 says most volunteers work weekends. Statement 5 counts all weekend workers, a different group. The volunteers who work weekends could be among the untrained weekend workers. Nothing requires most volunteers to be trained.\\r\\n\\r\\n**4. Yes.** A some statement describes an overlap in either direction: **some trained people are volunteers**, and **some weekend workers are students**.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n68:  .classroom-root .quantity-note > section > p,\\r\\n109:  .classroom-root .quantity-note .quantity-lab-slider { display: block; ## assistant

The v2 preview still begins with the original mediation opener, then inserts the concept extension afterward. Its builder explicitly renders the original opening before `integration-upgrade.md` and reuses a truth model keyed to “Should undergo mediation.” That preserves the question-centered structure even though the added prose is generic.

Recommended restructure:

1. **Title: “Conditional Must Be True: Facts, Rules, and Connections.”** Open with actual definitions: “A fact tells you what is true in a particular case. A rule tells you what must follow if a condition is met.” Immediately contrast:
   - Fact: “Maya’s application was submitted late.”
   - Rule: “Every late application requires approval.”
   Explain that the rule alone does not establish a late application or completed approval.
2. **Two methods at a glance.** Side-by-side visual examples: a marked case activating `Late → requires approval`, and rules joining `Late → requires approval → requires signature`. Use descriptive labels “Use a fact” and “Connect rules.”
3. **Translate the complete statement.** Teach required means right using fresh permission examples. Distinguish “requires approval” from “has approval,” and “may enter” from “does enter.” Introduce only/only if after the ordinary-English relationship is clear.
4. **Use the two legal starting points.** Teach A and not B with examples, followed by B and not A as inconclusive. Preserve the existing depth and counterexamples without requiring mediation vocabulary.
5. **Connect rules in the right direction.** Matching complete middle terms; invalid shared triggers/results; hidden connection after contraposition; no existence inference from rules alone.
6. **Keep the whole requirement.** AND/OR negation with a permission example. Preserve modality when contraposing. Present weaker versus stronger wording as a separate short boundary section.
7. **Mixed practice and exact assigned work.** Fresh standalone scenarios; answer explanations identify the legal move or give a concrete counterexample. Preserve the assignment plan.

The Some/Most/All reference’s useful design pattern is **prose explanation → concrete visual experiment → named distinction → local check**, repeated throughout. Its opening places a readable scenario beside a manipulable eight-book model; later it uses explanatory illustrations, rearrangeable groups, numbered sections, answer-as-you-go checks, and a closing sequential quiz. Copy this teaching rhythm and visual hierarchy, not its quantity-specific controls.

A useful conditional equivalent is a **four-case explorer** for “Every late application requires approval.” Two toggles control “Submitted late” and “Requires approval.” Show all four cases, highlight only `late + not requiring approval` as violating the rule, and explain the selected case in full English. Label the toggles as stipulated facts about the example; they must not imply those facts are established by the rule itself. This supports reversal, denial, and contraposition better than animation alone.

A second modest interaction can let the learner choose between `A → B; B → C`, `A → B; A → C`, and `A → C; B → C`. Only the first becomes a joined chain; the others show an explanatory counterexample. Include full-English labels alongside letters.

Skill gap: the skill requires a governing-concept opening and independence from remembered questions, but it does not enforce **generic definitions before source-specific examples**, or require the builder to replace a rejected opening. The existing builder compounds this by treating original teaching sections and the mediation model as fixed insertion anchors. Add a concrete quality gate: the opening defines the reusable distinction before any source-question wording; source examples support later explanation; visuals use fresh complete predicates; a revision reconstructs the student-facing sequence rather than appending an extension. Keep prior drafts as historical artifacts.

One reference caveat: the 08 builder checks typed responses with keywords and scores yes/no matches. Reuse the layout and interactions; keep reasoned answers as honest self-comparison unless the checking logic can actually evaluate them.
